• Бо̀жић Ба̏та - on the night before Christmas, January 7.
• Saint Nicholas (Ни̏кољдан) - in December.

The figure of Божић Бата is gradually merging with Деда Мраз and Santa Claus.

related.en: hot rakija, the Serbian counterpart of mulled wine
«Šumadija tea», another name for hot rakija
džezva, a small pot for Turkish coffee

note:
The Serbian counterpart of mulled wine is куване ракије, or шумадијски чај. It is drunk hot in winter.

How it is made:
1. Melt шѐћер (sugar) into caramel in a џезва.
2. Add the rakija.
3. When it comes to a boil, add a little water.

cyr: Serbian New Year and Mali Božić

related.en: василица: a special bread for St Basil's Day

note:
The «Old New Year» by the Julian calendar is called Српска нова година or Српска Православна нова година among Serbs. It is celebrated on 14 January.

This day is Ма̏лӣ Бо̀жић, or Василијевдан - the feast of St Basil the Great. A special bread, the васѝлица, is baked.

cyr: Срећан and сретан: Serbian and Croatian
note:
For «happy» in greetings, Serbs say сре̏ћан: Сре̏ћан Бо̀жић, срећна нова година. Croats say сре̏тан.

This is one of the most noticeable markers of the variant. In Serbian text use сре̏ћан.

related.en: to vibe, to be on the same wavelength
to ghost, to vanish without explanation

note:
Young people take English verbs and add Serbian endings:
• чиловати, кулѝрати - to chill
• вајбати - to vibe, to be on the same wavelength
• флексовати - to show off
• гоустовати - to ghost, to vanish without explanation
• кри̏нџ - secondhand embarrassment

Home-grown:
• «иде гас» - let's go, come on
• «скењ» - too bad, bummer

Сла̏вица on the Serbian internet is the counterpart of the Karen meme: a confrontational woman who lectures everyone about life.

Stickers also feature the fans of the Belgrade clubs:
• Делије - fans of Црвена звезда (Red Star), traditionally on the north stand
• Гробари - fans of Партизан, on the south stand

related.en: Stefan Nemanja, the father of St Sava

note:
On 27 January Serbia commemorates Saint Sava - Савиндан. Sava was the first archbishop of the Serbian Church and the son of Stefan Nemanja.

This is the school slava: there are no classes in schools on this day.

What Sava is known for:
• he founded the Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos
• he won independence for the Serbian Church in 1219

cyr: Мушко and женско in the neuter

related.en: a guy, a boy, a male (colloq.)
a woman, a girl, a female (colloq.)

related.sr: Овај коњ је мушко, а она је женско.
related.en: This horse is a male, and she is a female.
related.acc: О̀ва̄ј ко̏њ је му̏шко, а о̀на је жѐнско.

note:
In colloquial speech, the words мушко and женско (in the neuter gender) stand in for мушка́рац (man) and жѐна (woman):
• «Буди мушко!»
• «Она је право женско.»

They are also used of a newborn: «Родила је женско.» (She had a girl.)

And of animals: instead of му̏жја̄к and же̑нка - «Овај коњ је мушко, а она је женско.»

Belgrade Fortress (твр̀ђава) and Калемегдан are not the same thing:
• the fortress - the fortifications themselves
• Калемегдан - the park around it, laid out in the 19th century

The name is Turkish: кале - fortress, мѐјда̄н - open field. Serbs themselves use both words as synonyms.

The Ри̑мскӣ бу̀на̄р was built by the Austrians in the 18th century.

Ту̀рбофолк arose in late Yugoslavia from the новокомпонована народна музика of the 1970s and flourished in the 90s.

Features:
• folk motifs combined with dance and electronic rhythms
• lyrics about love and infidelity
• a flashy aesthetic

The first stars were Lepa Brena, then Ceca. Wartime turbofolk is a separate patriotic subgenre.

cyr: Pancakes the Serbian way: fillings and toppings

related.en: thick cream, similar to sour cream
a dairy product similar to sour cream

note:
Палачинке in Serbia are eaten both sweet and savory.

Savory fillings: ham and cheese, ground meat, salmon, caviar.

Sweet ones: nuts, almonds, coconut, шећер у праху (powdered sugar), jam, Nutella, еурокрем.

Close to sour cream here are па̀влака and милерам. One more topping is crushed «Plazma» biscuits.

related.en: the red Easter egg kept as a charm, the «house guardian»

note:
The first egg dyed for У̏скрс is red, and Serbs keep it until the next Easter. This is the чува̀ркућа - «house guardian»: according to belief, the egg protects the home and family.

It is not customary to throw it away after a year - better to bury it or throw it into running water.

The Easter greeting: «Христос васкрсе!» - «Ваистину васкрсе!»

related.en: SFRY, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
FPRY, the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia
FR Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia

related.sr: Државна заједница Србије и Црне Горе
related.en: State Union of Serbia and Montenegro
related.acc: Др̏жавна за̏једница Ср̀бије и Цр̏не Го̏ре

note:
Yugoslavia changed its name several times:
• Краљевина Срба, Хрвата и Словенаца - 1918-1929
• Краљевина Југославија - until 1941
• ФНРЈ - 1945-1963
• СФРЈ - 1963-1992
• СР Југославија - 1992-2003 (Serbia and Montenegro)
• Државна заједница Србије и Црне Горе - 2003-2006

Then it broke up into independent countries.

related.en: Vuk Karadžić, the reformer of the Serbian language

related.sr: пиши као што говориш, а читај као што је написано
related.en: write as you speak, and read as it is written
related.acc: пи́ши ка̏о што̏ го̀ворӣш, а чи̏тај ка̏о што̏ је написа̀но

note:
In the 18th century the Serbian literary language - славеносрпски - was a mix of Russian Church Slavonic and the spoken language. It differed greatly from the vernacular. Zaharija Orfelin and Milovan Vidaković wrote in it.

In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić rejected this and introduced the phonetic principle: «пиши као што говориш, а читај као што је написано» (write as you speak, and read as it is written).

related.en: Бијело дугме, a Yugoslav rock band
«Time of the Gypsies», a film by Kusturica

note:
On 6 May Serbs celebrate St George's Day - Ђу̏рђевда̄н. It marks the coming of spring (про̀леће).

The song of the same name by the band Бијело дугме is linked with it. There are two versions of its origin:
• it was born in the war years
• it is a Serbian version of the Romani «Ederlezi», made by Goran Bregović for Kusturica's film «Вре́ме Ци̏га̄на» (Time of the Gypsies)

In the Serbian translation the names are spelled the Serbian way: Хари Потер, Хогвортс, Волдемор.

Fun finds:
• нормалац - Muggle
• Смртождер - Death Eater
• Шѐшӣр за разврста́ва̄ње - the Sorting Hat
• Камен мудрости - the Philosopher's Stone
• Јецајућа Мирта - Moaning Myrtle
• ку̏ћнӣ вѝлењак - house-elf

A wizard is чаро̀бња̄к.

Instead of «well», «um» and «like», Serbs insert па, о̀ва̄ј, да̏кле̄, зна̏чи.

Other filler words are often heard too:
• «како се зове», оно
• у фазону, бра̏те
• ре̏а̄лно, бу̏ква̄лно
• види, зна̑ш, ми̏слӣм

The English «by the way» is also in use.

Видовдан is the day of St Vitus and the anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, between Prince Lazar and the army of Sultan Murad.

The battle ended without a clear winner, but became part of the Serbian self-image and folklore.

Other events that fell on Видовдан:
• the assassination of Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo (1914)
• the Видовдански устав of 1921
In many languages the «frog-eaters» are the French. In Serbian, жабари is the name for Italians: Italian cuisine also has frogs' legs.

cyr: Tearing the shirt of a new father

related.en: Tear it, bro, I've become a dad!

note:
Serbs have a tradition: when a man has a baby, his friends tear his clothes (це́пати). It symbolizes his new status and is a wish for strength and happiness.

There are even T-shirts made for this - «мајице за цепање».

The friends shout: «Цепај, брале, постао сам ћале!»

related.en: square pastries with meat or cheese

note:
Мантије are square pastries with meat or cheese, served with yogurt. They topped the TasteAtlas world ranking of savory baked goods. The Bosnian counterpart is буреџики (ranked lower).

Other Serbian pastries in the ranking:
• бу̀рек
• си́рница
• кромпируша
• зељаница

related.en: festival of dishes baked under a сач (a bell-shaped lid covered with embers)

note:
The ending -ијада means a food festival:
• роштиљијада - grill, Leskovac
• сачијада - dishes baked under a сач
• сиријада - cheese
• купусијада - cabbage
• штрудлијада - strudel
• чваркијада - cracklings, Valjevo
• ракијада - rakija

In 2024 the Leskovac festival entered the Guinness Book of Records because of a huge пљескавица.

related.en: SANU, the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts

note:
Abbreviations are read out in full: нпр. - на пример, итд. - и тако даље, тј. - то јест, тзв. - такозвани, бр. - број.

Acronyms are read in different ways:
• as a word: МУП, САНУ, УНЕСКО
• letter by letter: РТС, СПЦ, ЕУ, САД
• in full: ОШ - основна школа

Some are indeclinable (члан САНУ), others take case endings (чланице НАТО-а).

In Serbia Indian summer is called «михољско лето» after the feast of Михољдан (October 12). Real autumn is believed to begin after this date.

The feast is dedicated to St Cyriacus the Anchorite. The name may come from the Miracle of the Archangel Michael at Chonae, celebrated on September 19.

Several dubs of the cartoon have come out across the former Yugoslavia, and the Serbian version differs from the Croatian one.

Vocabulary: су̀нђер (sponge), ко̏цка (cube), ли̏гња (squid), пѝпак (tentacle), кле́шта (claws), бѝсер (pearl), ко̀рал (coral), шко̑љка (shell).

The name Коцкалоне means «square pants»: ко̏цка + пантало́не.

The word «vampire» is of Slavic origin. It is believed to have entered the European languages specifically from Serbian.

Serbian folklore has many evil creatures, for example караконџула - an evil spirit.

A Halloween joke: dress up as a караконџула, that is, go to bed with wet hair.

related.en: I do it for the pleasure of it

note:
Мѐра̄к is desire, enjoyment and unhurriedness: doing something without rush and with pleasure, even just drinking a cup of coffee or going to the shop.

The word is of Turkish origin, and it cannot be translated with a single word.

How people say it:
• «радим то из мерака»
• «нѝје ми мѐра̄к»

cyr: How to behave at a slava

related.en: feast of a family's patron saint

note:
Сла̏ва is the feast of a family's patron saint. It lasts three days, and relatives and friends come.

How a guest behaves:
1. Don't come empty-handed: bring sweets, coffee, wine or rakija, flowers.
2. Congratulate the host: «Срећна слава, домаћине!»
3. Cross yourself, offer your congratulations and help yourself to the food.

The hostess may serve жи̏то - a ritual dish of wheat, walnuts and honey. The дома̀ћин begins all the rites.

related.en: Children's Sunday, the third before Christmas
Mothers' Sunday, the second before Christmas
Fathers' Sunday, the last before Christmas

note:
On the three Sundays before Christmas, Serbia celebrates a family cycle:
• Детињци (the third Sunday) - adults symbolically tie up the children, who «ransom themselves» with a present, a song or a rhyme
• Материце (the second) - children tie their mother up with a ribbon, and she «ransoms herself» with sweets, nuts or small change; they give mum flowers and help around the house
• О̀ци (the Sunday before Christmas) - the same for fathers

related.en: 5 January, the eve of Christmas Eve
Christmas roast piglet on a spit

note:
Туциндан is 5 January. The name is linked with the verb ту́ћи (to beat): on this day a young piglet is slaughtered for the Christmas dish - божићна печеница.

Beliefs:
• children must not be beaten on this day, or they will misbehave all year
• in some places, on the contrary, children are symbolically pulled by the ears

Legend: under the Turks, Serbs roasted pork specifically so that Muslims would keep away from the house.

related.en: a shot of rakija in a mug of beer, «submarine»

note:
Home cocktails:
• шпри̏цер - white or rosé wine with soda water
• гѐмишт - wine with mineral water, but people more often call everything шприцер
• ба̀мбус - red wine with cola
• по̀дмо̄рница («submarine») - a shot of rakija in a mug of beer
• бушена вотка - vodka with juice, from the verb бу́шити (to drill)

Cola is considered the best cure for a hangover.

related.en: popara: bread, cheese and a hot liquid
parizer: a boiled sausage like bologna

note:
What Balkan children eat:
• плазма with milk - biscuits soaked in milk; plazma is eaten in every form
• по̀пара - bread, cheese and a hot liquid
• па̀ризер - something like bologna, often with bread

Па̀ризер became a political joke: Vučić ate it during an election campaign to show he was close to the people.

cyr: Syllabic R: Serbian is not a language without vowels
note:
A common myth: Serbian words have no vowels.

In fact the sound «р» can be syllabic and take the place of a vowel: чвр̑ст, ср̏пскӣ, тр̏жӣште, цр̑в.

Mastering it takes practice and a trilled tongue tip; it is not a matter of swallowing vowels.

On 14 February, besides Valentine's Day, Serbs celebrate Трифундан - the feast of Saint Tryphon, the patron of vine growers and winemakers.

On this day:
• the vines are pruned
• wine is drunk

The general word бу̏ба covers beetles and small insects.

The names:
• бубашва́ба - cockroach, «German bug»: the reddish-brown cockroach is thought to have come to the Balkans during the Austro-Turkish wars
• бубаруса - a related word, «Russian bug»: in popular speech, pests are often named after foreigners
• бубама́ра - ladybug, «Mary's bug», like the German Marienkäfer: it was linked with the Virgin Mary

cyr: How to say @, # and other symbols in Serbian
note:
Names of the symbols:
• @ - мајмунско а or лу̑до а
• # - тараба
• $ - до̏ла̄р, % - по̀стотак, & - зна̑к «и»
• / - ко̀са цр̏та, \ - обрнута коса црта
• _ - доња црта
• ' - а̀построф, ; - та̏чка-за̀рез, : - двотачка

Easter (У̏скрс or Ва̏скрс) is prepared for in advance:
• Вѐликӣ пе́так - a strict fast
• Велика субота - eggs are dyed; the first, red one is the чува̀ркућа, which protects the home until the next Easter
• Sunday - after the liturgy people knock eggs together to see whose shell is stronger

People bake the bread погача, and only the eggs are blessed. The main dish is roast lamb.

Easter Monday is the time to visit people.

A Sarajevo story about the «Ѝна̄т ку̏ћа» - the «house of spite». When the Austro-Hungarian authorities were building the city hall on the bank of the Miljacka, they decided to demolish the house of old Benderija.

He refused and demanded:
• to be paid in ducats
• to have his house moved to the other bank - brick by brick

The authorities agreed, and the house was nicknamed Ѝна̄т ку̏ћа. Now there is a Bosnian restaurant there.

At the market, nuts are sold by weight. The main names:
• о̀рах - walnut; it is also the tree
• ба́дем, ле̏шник, кикирѝки, пѝста̄ћ, пѝњоли

The rest are formed descriptively: индијски орах (cashew), бра̀зӣлскӣ о̀рах (Brazil nut).

Пекан, макадамија and ко̏кос sound as they do in English.

A kilim from the town of Pirot is recognized by its geometric patterns. The main motif is the eight-pointed star, a symbol of protection and fertility.

Other patterns:
• коларић
• бу̑рма
• бѝбер
• ло̀за

The oldest surviving kilim dates from 1650. These kilims were luxury items.

cyr: Which animals are insults in Serbia

related.en: male name, insulting as a form of address

note:
A Serb will not take offense at ја̏рац: it is a neutral word for a billy goat.

Insults for a man are instead:
• ма̀јмун
• ма̀гарац
• ко̏њ

Vocative: ма̀јмуне, магарче, коњу. Ма̀јмун is masculine, so you would not say it to a woman.

Also, Шабан is a name, but calling an adult «Шабане!» is a rude insult.

cyr: Fairy-tale and cartoon characters in Serbian

related.en: the snowman as a character, Frosty

note:
Many of the names are playful Serbian versions of the originals:
• Пепѐљуга
• Снежана
• Палчица
• Златокоса
• Душко Дугоушко
• Паја Патак
• Пера Детлић
• Сунђер Боб Коцкалоне - from ко̏цка (cube) and пантало́не (pants)
• Сне̏шко Бѐлић - «Бѐлић» looks like a surname

The English equivalents are in the related words.

cyr: Baba Roga, the Serbian Baba Yaga

related.en: Baba Roga, the Serbian Baba Yaga

note:
Serbs call Baba Yaga баба Рога.

A popular children's poem by Ljubivoje Ršumović is about a brave boy. The old woman lives in a пећина (cave) and hides in the dark. The boy brings her a lemon and a pear, and she will not even show her њушка: she is afraid of him.

The poem rhymes and is easy to learn by heart.

Serbs are keen on horoscopes and usually know not only their sign but also their rising sign (the ascendant).

The signs:
• Водолија, Рибе, О́ван, Би̏к
• Близа̀нци, Ра̏к, Ла̏в, Дѐвица
• Ва́га, Шкорпија, Стре́лац, Ја̏рац

A joke: «ду̏плӣ Ја̏рац» means a Capricorn by both sign and rising sign. It is almost a diagnosis, and nothing good is associated with it.

Short forms are not always predictable:
• Марија shortens to Мара and Маја, while Ма́ша is a separate name
• Јелена, Елена and Лена are different names
• Са̏ша is a male name, Ва̏ња is a full female name

Suffixes:
• -ка (Сашка, Машка) sounds warm
• -ица makes a diminutive (Машица)

Girls' names can also be fruits and berries: Ја̏года, Ви̏шња, Ма̀лина, Ду̏ња.

Documents ask for и̏ме, прѐзиме and и̏ме о̀ца (father's name).

A cat is called with «мац-мац» and a dog with «кс-кс»: the familiar «here, kitty» means nothing to a Serbian cat. For a cat there is also the diminutive ма́ца.

Sounds:
• па̏с ла̏је̄: ав-ав (woof)
• ма́ца мјауче и преде (meows and purrs)
• со́ва: ху-ху (hoot)
• кра̏ва: му (moo)
• гу̏ска: га-га (honk)
• пе́тао: кукурику (cock-a-doodle-doo)
• ко̀ко̄шка: ко̏-ко̏-ко̏ (cluck)
• пра̑се: грок-грок (oink)
• ко̏њ: њи-њи (neigh)
• ми̏ш: цију (squeak)
• пи̏ле: пи̏јӯ (peep)
• па̏тка: ква-ква (quack)
• жа̏ба: кре-кре (ribbit)

related.en: «The Seven Deadly Sins», a snack bar in Novi Sad

note:
In central Novi Sad there is a snack bar called «Седам смртних грехова»: every sandwich is named after a sin.
• го́рдо̄ст (pride), за́вист (envy), прождрљивост (gluttony)
• по̏жуда (lust), гне̑в (wrath), по̏хлепа (greed), ле̏њо̄ст (sloth)

On the door there is a pun: instead of дије́та it says дијете (child, in the ijekavian form). The result reads as «not the right place for a diet or for a child».

related.en: the time before noon, including the morning

note:
Approximate boundaries:
• ју̏тро - until 10 a.m.
• препо́дне - until noon (including the morning)
• по́дне - 12:00
• попо́дне - from 12 to 17
• ве̏че̄ - around 18-19
• по̏но̄ћ - 00:00

«Препо́дне» as one word is a part of the day, while «пре̏ по́дне» is a time phrase: before noon.

For seasons that have just passed, Serbs say ле̏то̄с, зѝмӯс, јесѐнас, про̀лето̄с: this summer, this winter and so on, once the season is over.

«На вре́ме» means on time.

Fingers (прсти):
• па̏лац
• ка̀жипрст - literally «pointing finger»
• сре̏дњӣ пр̏ст
• домали прст
• ма̏лӣ пр̏ст

The rest: пѐсница (fist), дла̏н (palm), ша̏ка (hand).

The wedding ring (бу̑рма) is worn on the домали прст; in Serbia Orthodox Christians wear it on the right hand.

In small towns a death is announced with a death notice (смр̀товница) on poles and notice boards.

A notice shows:
• a photo of the deceased
• the years of life
• the date and place of the funeral (са̀храна)
• the names of the grieving relatives

Newspapers have a similar section with photos.

The usual words of condolence: «Примите моје саучешће».

related.en: to cheer for, to root for

note:
Nicknames of the fans of the Belgrade clubs:
• гробари (gravediggers) - Partizan
• цигани - Red Star

The word хулигани is harsh: it is used for fans who riot. It is not used for a child.

Навѝјати means to cheer for a team: «За кога навијаш?»

On February 14 Serbia celebrates Дан заљубљених. In the church calendar this is the day of Све̑тӣ Три̏фӯн, the patron saint of vine growers and winemakers.

People wish each other «Срећан Дан заљубљених».

In Serbia taxis are ordered by phone.

What to tell the dispatcher:
• the street
• the building number
• the entrance (у̀лаз)

The apartment number and the destination are not needed. The car arrives within a few minutes, so call only when you are ready to leave.

In the car:
1. Say hello and give the address.
2. Check the fare on the meter: day, night or holiday.
3. Leave a tip by rounding up the amount.

Einstein was married to a Serbian woman, Mileva Marić, whom he met as a student in 1896.

So people joke:
• a foreigner married to a Serbian woman is a «ср̏пскӣ зе̏т»
• a foreign woman married to a Serb is a «српска снајка»

Many schools in Serbia are named after famous people instead of being numbered, Mileva Marić-Einstein among them.

In Serbia March 8 is a working day, but it is customary to give flowers, and restaurants hand them out to women.

Young people today often congratulate only their mother and their teacher.

On the eve, March 7, men are jokingly «congratulated» on the holiday that is about to begin.

cyr: Italian-sounding humor: «пар лавора и три канте»

related.en: a couple of basins and three buckets

note:
A joke for Serbian friends: say «пар лавора и три канте» fast, and it sounds like an Italian phrase.

Said slowly in Serbian it means «a couple of basins and three buckets». The words ла̏вор and ка́нта (bucket; ка́нта за смѐће is a trash can) came from Italian.

related.en: pre-election silence (the day of quiet before the vote)

note:
Basic election vocabulary:
• стра̏нка, па̀ртија - party
• бѝра̄ч, гла̀са̄ч - voter
• бирачко место - polling station
• изборна комисија - election commission
• гласачки листић - ballot
• гла̀сати, гла̀са̄ње - to vote, voting
• гласачко тело - electorate
• резултати гласања - voting results
• предизборна тишина - the quiet period before the vote

«Поно̀вити гла̀са̄ње» means to vote again.

related.en: the red egg kept as a protective charm

note:
At Easter (У̏скрс, church name Ва̏скрс) people greet each other with «Христос васкрсе!» - «Ваистину васкрсе!».

Customs:
• dyeing eggs (фарбати јаја, бојити јаја)
• red eggs must be on the table; one is kept until the next Easter as a charm (чува̀ркућа)
• playing «туцање јајима» (egg tapping, cracking eggs against each other)
• at night children put out a basket for the Easter bunny (ускршњи зец), who brings gifts

Serbia has a day of jokes on April 1 too: «Дан првоаприлске шале».

What people shout:
• after pulling a prank: «Априлилили!»
• at a good joke: «Ба̏ш је фо̏ра!»

A joke is a good way to start a conversation with Serbian friends.

related.sr: Еци, пеци, пец, ти си мали зец
related.en: Eci, peci, pec, you are a little hare
related.acc: Е̏ци, пе́ци, пе̑ц, ти си ма̑лӣ зе̑ц

related.sr: Ен ден доре, дубоко је море
related.en: En den dore, the sea is deep
related.acc: Е̑н де̑н до̏ре, дубо̀ко је мо̑ре

related.en: A duck swims across the Sava

note:
A counting-out rhyme is a «броја̀лица» in Serbian, from the word бро̑ј (number). Such rhymes are used in games like жму̏рке and «између две ватре» (dodgeball).

Classic openings:
• «Еци, пеци, пец, ти си мали зец»
• «Ен ден доре, дубоко је море»
• «Плива патка преко Саве»
• «Иде маца око тебе»

cyr: Taking off your shoes at someone's home
note:
In Serbian homes it is customary to take off your shoes at the door: «Изу́ва̄ње (ко̏д нас)!»

Hosts offer guests slippers (папу̀че), so shoes come off in other people's homes too. If the hosts themselves say «Не изувајте се», you can keep your shoes on.

The verb: ѝзути се (pf.), изу́вати се (impf.).

Someone who sneezes is told «На̀здравље!» - «bless you» (literally «to your health»).

Small children are sometimes told «Пис, мацо!» - «shoo, kitty!» as a playful reaction.

Words: ки́јати, ки́нути, кија̀вица.

A fan clenches a fist, chops the air with it and chants «Ср̀бија, Ср̀бија!»

For encouragement:
• «Идемо!»
• «А̀јмо, а̀јде сви̏ у на́пад!»
• «На̏пре̄д Ср̀бија!»
• «Го̑л!»

Partizan fans are гробари, Red Star fans are делије. The word «цигани» is considered offensive.

cyr: Serbian songs: women take revenge, men complain

related.en: I have the whole world under my heels

note:
You may notice that most popular songs sung by women are about «revenge on an ex»: look how happy I am without you. Songs sung by men are about complaints: «I loved you, and you left me».

An example is «Три чаше»: the heroine drinks to each of her loves and says «цео свет сам под штиклама».

Informal Serbian (especially among young people) has a slang, ша̏тровачкӣ го̏во̄р, in which the second part of a word is moved to the front.

Examples:
• здра̏во - воздра
• бра̏те - тебра
• за́кон - конза
• гла́ва - вугла
• пи̑во - вопи
• ва̏жи - жи̏ва
• ћа̏ле - ле́ћа

A catchphrase: «Мунзе конза» - «Zemun is the law».

In Serbian homes a guest is welcomed with слатко: a tray is brought out with preserves, teaspoons (кашичице) and two glasses of water.

How to enjoy it:
1. Take a spoonful of the preserve.
2. Put the used spoon into one of the glasses.
3. Wash it down with water from the other glass.

It is a sign of hospitality. Do not confuse it with сла̏ткӣ ку̀пус, braised cabbage with red pepper, a favorite dish.

cyr: Fruits, berries and the names of rakija
note:
The word во̀ће is collective: fruit and berries.

Rakija is named after the fruit it is made from:
• шљи̏ва - plums
• ка̀јсија - apricots
• кру̏шка - pears

So if you are offered a «кајсија» in winter, it is not an apricot.

Berries are usually plural: купине, малине, рибизле.

What to take on a trip, in Serbian:
• прѐхлада - a cold
• диареја - diarrhea
• лек против температуре - fever reducer
• a remedy for bites (у̏јед)
• фластери, га́за, за́вој - adhesive bandages, gauze, bandage
• remedies for nausea and vomiting (мучнина, повраћање)
• a medicine for a sore throat (упала грла)
• креме са заштитним фактором и после сунчања - sunscreen and after-sun cream

A send-off wish: «Сре̏ћан пу̑т!»

related.en: «Браћу не доносе роде» («Storks don't bring brothers»), a children's song

note:
The children's song «Браћу не доносе роде» lists Serbian regions: Сре̑м and Ба̑нат. Both are in Војво̀дина, in the north.

The text also has:
• «купус из Срема» - mentioned as a joke
• ду̀ћа̄н - shop
• по̀родилиште - maternity hospital

Small boys, strangers' or one's own, are addressed as «бато!», girls as «се́ка», a son or a daughter as «си̑не!».

Кли̑нци means kids. The word бра̏т has a broad meaning in Serbian: it can be used for any male relative.

More words: новоро̀ђе̄нче, бе́ба, малѝшан.

The favorite place of Serbs is Greece: Halkidiki (Kassandra) and the islands of Thasos, Zakynthos, Skiathos and Кр̏ф (Corfu).

Other destinations:
• Montenegro is seen as close and not very interesting; Бу̑два is for young people
• in Turkey - Kuşadası and Marmaris
• at home - thermal spas (бање: Врњачка Бања, Сокобања, Про̀лом Ба̏ња) and mountains (Та̏ра, Златибор, Копаоник)

Duty free is called «фри шоп».

related.en: right into someone's ear (of musicians playing up close to one guest)

note:
Трубачи are folk brass bands whose playing sets the mood at weddings and in кафане (traditional taverns).

They do not play for free: when the band comes to your table, it is customary to give them money, sometimes even tucking it into the trumpet.

The song «Нѐсаница» is from the repertoire that is often played «на увце», right into a guest's ear.

cyr: Brand names used as common nouns
note:
Like «Kleenex» or «Band-Aid» in English: a brand has become the common name.
• any toothpaste is каладонт (калодо̏нт)
• any chocolate spread is еурокрем (Nutella too)
• any adhesive bandage is хансапласт, although Serbian also has the word фла̏стер

Patterns on clothes:
• ша́ра, дѐзен - a pattern in general
• штрафте - stripes
• туфне, туфнице - polka dots
• ка̏ро (карирана кошуља) - checks
• цвѐтнӣ дѐзен - floral
• једнобојна одећа - plain clothes
• камуфлажни дезен, војнички дезен - camouflage, military print

Special names: «ћуркице» - paisley, «пепито» - houndstooth.

related.sr: Још једна песма о малој гаравој
related.en: «Још једна песма о малој гаравој» («Another Song About the Little Dark-Haired Girl»)
related.acc: Јо̏ш је̏дна пе̏сма о ма̏лој га̏равој

related.sr: мала гарава, црна као браћа Арапи
related.en: a little dark-haired girl, black as our Arab brothers
related.acc: ма̏ла га̏рава, цр̏на ка̏о бра̏ћа Ара̀пи

note:
In Đorđe Balašević's song «Још једна песма о малој гаравој» blondes are called:
• крво̀пије
• анаконде
• дражесни паразити
• барбике

The hero wants «малу гараву, црну као браћа Арапи» instead.

The song shows a playful, self-ironic attitude to types of women.

Serbian also names teeth by numbers:
• «једѝнице и дво̏јке» - incisors (секутићи)
• «тро̏јке» - canines (очњаци)
• «чѐтворке и пѐтице» - premolars (преткутњаци)
• «шестице, седмице, осмице» - molars (кутњаци)

The eighth is the у̏мњак (wisdom tooth).

Baby teeth are мле̑чнӣ, permanent ones ста̑лнӣ.

По̀врће means vegetables.

Onions are told apart by color:
• цр̑нӣ лу̏к - the common onion (literally «black onion»)
• бе̑лӣ лу̏к - garlic (literally «white onion»)
• црвени лук - red onion
• млади лук - green onion
• пра̀зилук - leek

Peppers:
• па̀прика - the vegetable
• ба̀бура - bell pepper
• љута паприка - hot pepper
• бѝбер - black pepper

Also: ро̀тквица - radish, ре̏н - horseradish, ти̏квица - zucchini.

In Serbia September 1 is Дан знања: the start of the school year.

Someone who celebrates every holiday is said to «слави све живо»: celebrates anything and everything.

related.en: a good catch (said by a woman)

note:
Colloquial words for men:
• шме̏кер - a charming ladies' man
• фа̑ца - a rich, arrogant macho
• фра̑јер - a good catch (said by a woman)
• папу̀чар - a henpecked husband
• ма̀нгуп - a scamp
• ло́ла - a womanizer
• бѝта̄нга - a scoundrel
• бара̀ба - a troublemaker
• зве̏рка - a big shot

A neutral one is «госпо̀дин чо̏век»: a decent man.

Salon services:
• депила̀ција ног (целих или пола), рук, пре̏пона, пазуха, наусница, ле́ђа, гру̑ди - hair removal of the legs (full or half), arms, groin, armpits, upper lip, back, chest
• бразилска депилација - Brazilian waxing

Types of wax: хла̑днӣ (cold), топли (hot). Шећерна паста is sugaring.

related.sr: имам заказано код фризера у суботу
related.en: I have an appointment at the hairdresser's on Saturday
related.acc: ѝма̄м за̀казано ко̏д фризѐра у су̀боту

note:
A popular service in Serbia is фени̏ра̄ње: a wash and blow-dry, straightened or curled. It is inexpensive.

You book ahead: «имам заказано код фризера у суботу».

Ши̏ша̄ње is a haircut. «Траје сат времена» means it takes an hour.

related.sr: Желим ти да добијеш све што немаш, а желиш. И задржиш све што имаш, а волиш.
related.en: I wish you to get everything you don't have but want, and to keep everything you have and love.
related.acc: Жѐлим ти да до̀бијеш све̏ што̏ не̑маш, а жѐлиш. И за̀држиш све̏ што̏ и̏маш, а во̏лӣш.

related.sr: Желим ти океане здравља, мора среће и љубави, језера успеха, реке пара...
related.en: I wish you oceans of health, seas of happiness and love, lakes of success, rivers of money...
related.acc: Жѐлим ти океа̀не здра̏вља, мо̏ра сре̏ће и љу́бави, је̏зера у̀спеха, рѐке па̑ра...

note:
Sample wishes (the translations are in the related words):
• «Желим ти да добијеш све што немаш, а желиш. И задржиш све што имаш, а волиш.»
• «Желим ти океане здравља, мора среће и љубави, језера успеха, реке пара...»

Children's birthdays are often held in a рођендаоница (a play room for parties). A song: «Ди̑ван да̑н».

Words: чѐститка, по́зӣвница, по̀клон, то̑рта.

cyr: Parts of the body: head and face
note:
The vocabulary topic «Човек» (the human being): гла́ва, чѐло, ли́це, о̀браз, о̏брва, но̑с, у́ста, у̏сна, нѐпце, јѐзик, јаго̀дице, гр̏ло, ждре́ло, у̏хо.

Gender quirks:
• о̏ко is neuter, but о̏чи (eyes) is feminine: лепе очи, њене очи
• уши is also feminine: његове уши
• у́ста is neuter and plural

cyr: At the bakery: what пециво is

related.en: rolled pie of thin dough with meat or cheese

note:
The basis of the Serbian diet is bread, meat and yogurt.

In a bakery everything baked is пѐциво, either сла̑но (savory) or сла̀тко̄ (sweet):
• ђѐврек - a sesame bagel
• ки́фла - a roll for sandwiches
• погачица са чварцима - a bun with cracklings (чва̏рци)
• бу̀рек - a rolled pie of thin dough with meat or cheese
• мѐкика - a fried oblong doughnut
• ка̀јзерица - a dense roll

related.en: the company that made scratch-off lottery tickets

note:
Греб-греб (from грѐбати, to scratch) was the name of a company that made scratch-off lottery tickets. The name became generic: any such tickets are called that. The general word for them is сре̏ћка.

The slogan «Огреби срећу!» plays on the meaning of сре̏ћа: both happiness and luck.

related.en: to get tanned, literally «to turn black»
to get tanned, literally «to get color»

note:
In Serbia a tan is a sign that a person has had a good rest. It is customary to say to a tanned acquaintance:
• «Баш сте поцрнели»
• «Добила си боју»

Literally поцр̀нети means «to turn black», but it sounds like praise.

In Montenegro and in ijekavian dialects people say ђе̏ instead of где̏. The famous Montenegrin song «Ђе се купаш?» parodies the speech of young men on the beach.

It mixes ijekavian forms with standard ekavian ones:
• смје̏шта̄ј - сме̏шта̄ј
• ље̏то - ле̏то
• мјеста - ме̑ста̄

related.en: to smell (give off a scent); to sniff
to rent (as a tenant); to rent out

note:
Serbian has words that mean two opposite things:
• мирѝсати - both to give off a smell and to smell something
• поза́јмити - both to borrow and to lend
• изна́јмити - both to rent and to rent out

The context shows which is meant, but even bilinguals mix up the direction of the action because of this.

На̀родњак is popular Serbian music in a folk spirit: it is sung at weddings and in the кафана.

Turbo-folk is a later style with modern arrangements and explicit lyrics.

Many hits were written to Greek melodies, and vice versa.

Nurseries (ја̀слице) take children up to three, then comes the вр̀тић (also о̀бданиште, за̀бавӣште).

The last year before school is the прѐдшколско: school preparation, required by law.

Kindergartens get cute names: Ба̑јка, Бубама́ра, Ве̏верица, Ду́га, Зво̀нчић, Масла́чак, Су̑нце, Чаро̀лија.

A kindergarten teacher is a васпѝтач or васпита̀чица, a nanny is да̀диља.

Halloween is seen as a Catholic holiday, and in Serbia it is observed mostly where it pays: shops, bars, clubs. There is no craze.

Asked about «но̑ћ вѐштица», a Serb often replies with irony, as if to say, what Halloween?

But the Serbian words on the topic are worth knowing: баба Рога, вуко̀длак, ши̏шмиш, стра̏шило.

related.en: family feast of the patron saint

note:
Сла̏ва is the day of the family's patron saint. Each family keeps its own slava, and the date and customs pass from generation to generation. The feast is usually held in the home of the senior man of the family.

Always on the table:
• a candle
• славска погача
• red wine
• ко̏љӣво

An invitation is an honor: declining is not done, and once you have gone, it is polite to invite the hosts to your own slava in return.

Gifts: alcohol for the host, flowers or coffee for the hostess, chocolate for the children.

cyr: Commands for a dog in Serbian
note:
In Serbia a cat is called with «мац-мац», a dog with «кс-кс», and a dog barks «ав-ав».

Commands:
• «дођи!» - come here
• «седи!», «лези!» - sit, lie down
• «ста̏ни!» or «сто̑ј!» - stay
• «уз ногу!» - heel
• «пу̑стӣ!» - let go
• «остави то!» - leave it
• «ку̏ћи!» - go home

Praise: «до̏бар па̏с!», «бра̏во!»

To send a dog away: «бежи тамо!», or ruder, «мрш!»

related.en: the second evening of New Year, January 1
family feast of the patron saint

note:
In Serbia New Year is a cheerful holiday but not the main one: Сла̏ва, Бо̀жић and У̏скрс matter more.

How it is celebrated:
1. The celebration (до̀чек) starts in the daytime, with дневне журке in bars: tables are booked in advance, and there is live music.
2. Toward evening many people go home to rest.
3. At midnight they go to the square for a concert and ва̏тромет (fireworks).

The evening of January 1 is the реприза Нове године, a second holiday.

Gifts are mostly for children.

related.en: young oak branches burned on Christmas Eve
the first guest in the house

note:
January 6 is Бадњи дан, the last day of the fast. In the evening people burn the ба̏дња̄к: young oak branches.

January 7 is Бо̀жић, the main family holiday; shops are closed.

On the table at lunch:
• sprouted wheat
• a candle
• цѝцвара
• че̏сница with a coin

The first guest is the по̀ложајник.

The greeting: «Христос се роди!» - «Ваистину се роди!»

related.en: family feast of the patron saint

note:
Besides the family Слава, there is also a Slava of a city or a school.

Cities:
• Belgrade - Спасовдан
• Novi Sad - Ђурђиц

This is not Дан града (City Day), so do not mix them up.

Schoolchildren have their own Slava - Са̀виндан, St Sava's Day, 27 January: no lessons, and the pupils put on concerts. Да̑н сту̀дена̄та̄ (Students' Day) is 4 April.

On 14 February people split into two camps: some celebrate St Trifun's Day (Трифундан), others Valentine's Day (Дан заљубљених).

Све̑тӣ Три̏фӯн is the patron saint of winemakers, and on this day the vines (ло̏за) are pruned.

Couples send each other rhymed text-message confessions.

related.en: little rascal, ringleader (said of a boy, jokingly)

note:
Serbs know how to call children tenderly: «зла̑то» (gold), «срце мамино» (mommy's heart), «мѝшӣћ» (little mouse), «бубица» (little bug), «лепо̀тица» (beauty), «слаткица» (sweetie), «шѐћер» (sugar), «паху̀љица» (snowflake), «мѐзимица» (darling), «шећерле̏ма» (sweet tooth).

A boy is jokingly called «харамба̀ша», and a spoiled child «мамина маза».

Годишња доба: про̀леће, ле̏то, је̏се̄н, зи́ма. A Serb lists the seasons starting with spring.

There are special adverbs for the past: ле̏то̄с, јесѐнас, зѝмӯс, про̀лето̄с (last summer, autumn, winter, spring).

Also:
• «михољско лето» - Indian summer
• «преступна година» - leap year

People jokingly speak of a «тринаеста плата» (a thirteenth salary) in state jobs.

related.en: a glass of rakija as a welcome

note:
A guest is welcomed with «ракија добродошлица» - a glass of rakija as a greeting.

To thank someone, you invite them «на кафу» (кафа захвалница) or to lunch. A gift can be chocolate, a bottle of alcohol, a souvenir or a present for the children.

On receiving a gift, Serbs open it at once in front of the giver and express surprise: «Јао, није требало…»

School in Serbia:
• a генера́ција (age cohort) runs from 1 March to 28 February: everyone born in that period starts school in the same year
• the year before school is a compulsory preparatory group (прѐдшколско)
• о̀сновна шко̑ла lasts 8 years (4+4)
• then срѐдња шко̑ла: a гѝмна̄зија for 4 years or a vocational school for 3
• pupils study for 12 years in all

Children first write in Cyrillic, then Latin is added. They write in pencil and there is no school diary. Serbs picture the week as a row of days, not a circle.

related.en: house guardian (an egg kept for a year)

note:
In Serbia people do not bake Easter cakes, so they dye and bless eggs (фарбати јаја).

Customs:
• red eggs are a must on the table, and one of them is kept until the next Easter as a «чува̀ркућа»
• children play «туцање јајима» (egg tapping)
• the bunny (ускршњи зец) brings gifts in a basket: the day before, children gather grass for it

The greeting: «Христос васкрсе!» - «Ваистину васкрсе!».

related.en: sour cherry, also a woman's name
a woman's name (felt to be Russian)
Petar Petrović, the Serbian counterpart of John Smith

note:
Suffixes:
• -ка does not make a name rude, on the contrary it is affectionate: Сашка, Машка, Мирка
• -ица gives a tender form: Машица, Ољица

Many women's names are berries and fruits: Ја̏года, Ви̏шња, Ма̀лина, Ду̏ња.

The Serbian counterpart of John Smith is Пѐтар Пѐтровић.

Ве̏ра, На́да, Љу́бав are Faith, Hope and Love.

related.en: the first half of the day (before noon)

note:
Serbs divide the day roughly like this:
• ју̏тро̄с - morning, about 3-9 am
• препо́дне - before noon
• у по́дне - 12 noon
• попо́дне - after lunch until 3 pm
• послепо́дне - about 3-7 pm
• ве̏че̄ - 7-11 pm
• у по̏но̄ћ - midnight

The boundaries are loose.

For «tomorrow» the same words go with су̏тра: су̏тра у̀јутру, су̏тра попо́дне, су̏тра у̏вече̄.

Also: пре̏кјуче̄ - the day before yesterday, преко̀сутра - the day after tomorrow.

Titles of Russian books are often translated into Serbian:
• «Ра̏т и ми̑р»
• «Зло̀чин и ка̏зна»
• «Ју̀на̄к на̏ше̄г до̑ба»
• «Мртве душе»
• «Тешко паметном»
• «Вишњик»
• «Галеб»
• «Дама са псетанцетом»
• «Зли̑ ду̏си»
• «Мајстор и Маргарита»

Surnames are spelled differently: Достојевски, Гогољ, Љермонтов.

Eateries are named after the main dish plus the suffix -ница or -џиница, which marks a place:
• ћевабџѝница - ћевапи
• бурегџѝница - burek
• палачѝнкарница - pancakes
• посластѝчарница - pastry shop

cyr: Syllabic R: words almost without vowels

related.en: tongue twister: On top of the hill the willow sways

note:
In Serbian the letter «р» can be a vowel sound, so a word can do without vowels: вр̏т, пр̏ст, кр̑в, смр̏т, кр̏ст, бр̑з, ср̏це, цр̑ква, Ср̀бија.

The sound can be drawn out, like a growl.

For practice there is a tongue twister: «На врх брда врба мрда».

cyr: Countries and cities in the names of things
note:
Serbian names many things after peoples and cities, and not always the way English does:
• јапа̀нке - flip-flops
• фра̀нцӯскӣ крѐвет - a double bed
• амѐричкӣ пла̀кар - a built-in wardrobe
• шве̏дскӣ сто̑ - a buffet
• руска салата - Russian salad (Olivier)
• ру̏скӣ ча̏ј - black tea
• па̀ризер - a boiled sausage like bologna
• венецијанери - blinds
• шпанска села - something incomprehensible (literally «Spanish villages»)

Serbian sounds:
• клај-клај - choo-choo (a train)
• куц-куц - knock-knock
• пу-пу-пу - touch wood (said with a knock)
• фу̏ј, бља̏к - yuck
• пих - what a stink
• пст - shh
• ауч - ouch
• ср̑к - slurp
• хрк - snore
• хик - hiccup
• цмок - smooch
• ју̀пи - yippee

Animals are called and chased away with different words:
• мац-мац - to call a cat
• чи̏бе - to chase a dog
• ши̏ц - to chase a cat

Ма̏ јо̏к means «of course not», но но means «tut-tut». After a sneeze people say «На̀здравље».

Words for a corner and a dead end:
• ћо̀шак - a corner, from Turkish, colloquial
• со̀ка̄к - a lane; today found in songs or used ironically
• ћорсо̀ка̄к - a dead end; in everyday speech it is replaced by the calque слепа улица
• ку́так - a cozy nook, a rare word

The neutral word for a corner is у̏гао.

Colors that surprise:
• пла̑ва - blue, light blue and blond at once: пла̑ва ко̀са, пла̀вуша
• црвена коса - red (ginger) hair
• црно вино - red wine (literally «black wine»)
• модра - dark blue, мо̏дрица - a bruise
• тѐгет - a dark navy that is almost black
• смеђа and бра̏он - brown; смеђе очи - brown eyes
• жута минута - a momentary lapse (literally «a yellow minute»)

Many neutral Serbian words are made of two roots:
• главо̀боља - head + pain
• зубо̀боља, врто̀главица
• пољопрѝвреда - field + farming
• мравојед, пуно̀главац
• чува̀ркућа - houseleek

Some words are emotionally colored: пу̏столо̄в, сладоку́сац, да̏нгуба, вѐтропир, цепѝдлака, про̀бисвет, џа̀балебарош, ра̀спикућа, брзо̀плет, тврдо̀глав.

cyr: New Year in Serbia: the daytime party

related.en: the second evening of New Year, 1 January
family feast of the patron saint

note:
New Year in Serbia is more modest than Christmas and Slava.

How it is celebrated:
1. It starts in the daytime on 31 December: people book a table at a bar in advance, there may be an entrance fee, and live music plays (дневна журка).
2. By evening many go home to rest.
3. The evening of 1 January is called реприза Нове године.

Gifts go mostly to children.

cyr: Five working words for everyday talk
note:
Five working words for everyday talk:
• Може - agreeing to an offer: «Може ли ракија?» - «Може!»
• Ва̏жи - «all right, deal» in reply to a suggestion
• Хо̀ћу - «I'll do it», a stand-alone answer to a request
• Ни̏шта (ма̏ ни̏шта) - the answer to an apology or thanks
• Гу̑жва - traffic jams and crowds; «У гу̑жвӣ сам» explains both forgetfulness and being busy

In Serbian society men are praised not only for what they do but also for how they look: you may hear «ле̑п ка̏о лу̏тка» (pretty as a doll).

«Good-looking» to a Serb means neat, well groomed, tall, not heavy.

Praise for character:
• сна́жан, духо̀вит, бри̏жан, о̏дгово̄ран
• по̀штен, хра́бар, о̏длӯчан, у̏по̄ран

related.en: a town whose whole name fits on a plate

note:
Serbian license plates carry two letters, the city code:
• BG - Београд
• NS - Нови Сад
• NI - Ниш
• KG - Крагујевац
• SU - Суботица

RU is Рума, not Russia. Only the town of Уб has its whole name on the plate (UB).

Montenegro also uses city codes: PG - Подгорица, BD - Будва. Bosnia has had no city codes since 1998, only letters that are written the same in both alphabets.

Serbian has about 8000 active Turkisms:
• ча̀рапа, ко̀мшија, џе̏п, ду̀гме
• ја̀стук, то́рба, буда̀ла, џа̏бе̄

From German came бѝна, ки́фла, фле̏ка, ци́гла, шпо̏рет, штѝкла, шра̀фцӣгер.

From Italian: пѝјаца, ру́жа, о̏пера. From Hungarian: гу̏ла̄ш, со̏ба, чи̏зме.

A henpecked husband is called папу̀чар, from па̀пуча (slipper).

Many Serbian words are adjectives that became nouns:
• запо̏сленӣ - employee
• надре̏ђенӣ - superior
• подређени, дежу̏рнӣ, осу̏мњиченӣ, ухапшени

Short everyday names arose the same way: до̀ма̄ћӣ (homework), во̀зачка (driver's license), хитна (ambulance), да̀љӣнскӣ (remote control), ку̀па̄ћӣ (swimsuit).

They decline like adjectives: о новом запосленом.

cyr: Names of famous people in Serbian
note:
Serbian renders foreign names by sound:
• Конфучије, Бу́да, Питагора, Микеланђело
• Џорџ Вашингтон, Виктор Иго, Алберт Ајнштајн, Ле Корбизије
• Јованка Орлеанка (Joan of Arc), Па̑па Фра̏ња (Pope Francis), Луј (Louis)

Rulers are named like this: Пѐтар Вѐликӣ (Peter the Great), Катарина Велика (Catherine the Great).

In Serbia many characters go by their own names:
• Bugs Bunny - Душко Дугоушко
• Donald Duck - Паја Патак
• Goofy - Шиља
• Scrooge McDuck - Ба́ја Па́так
• Woody Woodpecker - Пера Детлић
• Tinker Bell - Звончица
• Captain Hook - Ку̏ка

Others stayed as they are: Том и Џери, Петар Пан, Шре̏к.

A bogeyman or monster in Serbian is ба̀ук.

You can call a Serb a ко̏њ, ма̀гарац or ма̀јмун, but not a goat: ја̏рац is Capricorn from the horoscope, and the Serb will simply think you mean his sign.

People use the vocative: Коњу! Магарче! Ма̀јмуне! The last one is considered very insulting.

You can make it stronger: Коњу један!

cyr: Words that exist only in the plural
note:
Serbian has words that exist only in the plural:
• neuter: вра́та, ле́ђа, ко̏ла
• гру̑ди, дѐснӣ, на̏оча̄ре, пантало́не
• фа̀рмерке, га̏ће, но̀вине, ме̏рдевине
• feminine: гра̀буље

They agree as plurals: ова врата су дрвена, у овим фармеркама, ићи колима.

related.en: utilities: water, central heating, garbage collection, stairwell cleaning

note:
On the bills look for:
• рачун за струју, грѐја̄ње, во̀да, и̏нтернет
• и̏нфостан - utilities: water, central heating, garbage collection, stairwell cleaning

Electricity is split into вишу тарифу (daytime, ску̏па стру́ја) and нижу (nighttime, јѐфтина стру́ја).

Further down the bill:
• бро̀јило, потро̀шња
• у̀купно за пла́ћа̄ње, ро̏к за пла́ћа̄ње
• ка̏мата - late fee

related.en: I know it from A to Z

note:
Besides Cyrillic (ћирѝлица) and Latin (латѝница), people in messages write «bald» Latin - ћелавица:
• no marks: c instead of č and ć, s instead of š, z instead of ž
• dj instead of đ

This causes mistakes: cackalica is чачка̀лица (toothpick), kuce is ку̏че (puppy) or ку̏ћа (house) depending on the context.

The alphabet has 30 letters, from «А» to «Ш»: «знам од А до Ш».

Serbs depend a lot on the weather: in bad weather it is easy to cancel a meeting, but on a sunny weekend you cannot get into a restaurant without a booking, especially on an open terrace.

Call in the morning of the same day.

When the table is booked, you hear «Резервисано је!» Before eating: «При̏ја̄тно!»

cyr: The music code of a Serbian wedding
note:
At a Serbian wedding a live band (жи̏ва сви̑рка) sets the mood.

The usual order:
1. world hits
2. Yugoslav rock (југорок)
3. popular folk songs
4. modern hits
5. ту̀рбофолк for the dance floor, and севдалинке

Towards morning the repertoire gets less picky. The hosts' task is to please the guests with food and music.

related.en: volleyball player; Vanja is the name he is known by
short for Svetislav (also a male name)

note:
In Serbia an athlete may be written with two names: Владимир Вања Грбић, where Ва̏ња is the name he is known by.

Unexpected names:
• Страхиња - male
• Љу́ба - short for Љу̏бомӣр
• Света - from Све̏тислав, also male
• Ва̏ња is more often female

Other common names: Мима, Немања, Не̏на̄д, Бо̀јан.

Пара̀дајз турѝзам is the ironic name for a kind of holiday where food is brought from home to the beach: canned goods, vegetables, sausage, tomatoes. The term appeared in the early 1980s, when holidays in Greece became popular.

Serbs spend the whole day on the beach: they arrive around ten and leave last. They complain about the heat («на̏пољу је па̀као») but do not hide from the sun.

cyr: Човек - a person and a man

related.sr: Само нек је живо и здраво.
related.en: As long as it's alive and well.
related.acc: Са̏мо не̑к је жи̑во и здра̏во.

note:
The word чо̏век means both «person» and «man», so for a woman people say о̏соба: она је оптимистична особа.

Forms of address for children: to a son - си̑не, to a daughter - ће̏ро, but a daughter is often addressed as си̑не too.

What people say about a newborn:
• a boy - «Прво, па мушко!»
• a girl - «Само нек је живо и здраво.»

In invitations the woman's name is written first.

Ко̀шава is a strong, gusty south-east wind. It often blows in Belgrade and northern Serbia, most of all in autumn and winter.

It brings clear, cold weather and raises dust and snow. People complain about it as a weather phenomenon linked with headaches and tiredness.

Serbian habits:
• they see no difference between tiger and leopard patterns - it is all «тиграсто»
• they love tracksuits
• they praise everything with the word ле̑по (nice, good, tasty)
• they peel cucumbers
• they do not like taking their shoes off
• at the first sign of a cold, the first thing is chamomile tea
• boiled milk is covered with a plate

They fear a draft (про̏маја), and «со̑к» also covers fizzy drinks.

related.en: to register at the employment office

note:
Familiar ones: по̏шта, полѝција, бо́лница, шко̑ла, вр̀тић, су̑д.

Special ones:
• о̏пштина - the municipality, also the registry office
• месна заједница - the local community council
• ску̏пштина - parliament or a city assembly
• би̏ро - the employment office: прија́вити се на би̏ро
• со̏ција̄лно - social welfare; РФЗО - the health insurance fund
• за́вод - an institution

Public utilities: Градска чистоћа (garbage collection), Градско зеленило (parks), Путеви Србије (roads).

related.sr: Нека ти се све жеље испуне!
related.en: May all your wishes come true!
related.acc: Не̏ка ти се све̏ же̏ље испу̀не!

note:
Serbs do not make long toasts: just «Жѝвели!»

Celebrations are more modest, without long feasts:
• cake and coffee on the table, snacks, often grilled meat
• bringing flowers is not customary

Congratulations are short: «Сре̏ћан ро̏ђенда̄н!», «Све̏ на̑јбоље!», «Нека ти се све жеље испуне!»

The 18th and 50th birthdays get special attention, and when a baby is born the father treats his friends.

related.en: nickname for a woman from Vojvodina
nickname for a man from Vojvodina

note:
These came from Hungarian:
• бу̑нда, ва́рош, ва́шар, кѐцеља
• ло́пов, ма̏чка, пу́нђа, са̏ла̄ш
• со̏ба, ци̏пеле, чо̏по̄р, чи̏зме

Many Hungarians live in Vojvodina, and in 30 municipalities Hungarian is an official language.

Women of Vojvodina are jokingly called соса, men - ла̏ла.

related.en: summer version of ајвар with eggplant and tomatoes
a biscuit that no childhood is without

note:
Unfamiliar to a newcomer:
• а̀јва̄р and its summer version пѝнђур
• ки̏селӣ ку̀пус, кисело млеко, про̀ја, ка̀јмак
• чва̏рци, пр̏шута
• плазма - a biscuit that no childhood is without

Зе̏ље is sorrel or spinach, коре за питу are pastry sheets for pie.

The numbers used to have two digits: police 92, fire brigade 93, ambulance 94. Now they are preceded by 1:
• полѝција - 192
• ватрогасци - 193
• хитна помоћ - 194

From a landline you could also dial 95: a machine announced the exact time, and an operator could wake you up on request. This is what the song «Окрени број 95» by the band Tap 011 is about.

related.en: and that's the end of the story

note:
Serbs love rhyming doublings:
• ти̑п-то̏п (all great), туто комплето (all together), цикцак (zigzag)
• ђа̑к пр̀ва̄к (first-grader), касица-прасица (piggy bank)
• хокус-покус, ћирибу-ћириба - a magician's spell
• еци-пеци-пец - a counting-out rhyme
• икс-окс, крѝжић-кру́жић - tic-tac-toe
• рус-купус, муж-пуж - just for the rhyme

A fairy tale ends with «чича Мича, готова прича».

cyr: Names that are also Serbian words
note:
These names are the same as Serbian words: Ду̏ња (quince), Ла̏ла (tulip), Лу́ка (port), На́на (mint), Вла́да (government), Сла̏ва (fame), Ри́ма (rhyme), Со̀фа (sofa), Ка̀мила (camel), Паша (pasture), Фо̏ка (seal), Ми̏ла (dear).

The names themselves are not translated, but they may make a Serb smile.

In Serbia a сла̏ва belongs not only to a family but also to a city, a church, a school, a trade and a company. Do not confuse it with City Day (Дан града).

Belgrade:
• Slava - Спасовдан (the 40th day after Easter)
• City Days - 16-19 April
• 20 October - Liberation Day

Novi Sad:
• Slava - Ђурђиц, 16 November
• City Day - 1 February

The school Slava is Савиндан, 27 January.

related.en: Repetition is the mother of learning.
Mom will call to excuse the absence.

note:
Grades run from 1 to 5:
• о̏дличан - 5
• вр̏ло до̏бар - 4
• до̏бар - 3
• до̏во̄љан - 2
• не̏дово̄љан - 1

A two is a pass and a one is a fail, hence the teacher's «Седи, један!».

More school phrases:
• «Загреј ту столицу!» - sit there until you have learned it
• «Понављање је мајка знања» - repetition is the mother of learning
• «Зваће мама да оправда» - Mom will call to excuse the absence

An address goes: street, house number, у̀лаз (entrance), спра̏т (floor), ста̑н (apartment).

In a long building each entrance has its own house number: entrance 3 - number 35, entrance 2 - number 34.

Floors are counted from zero: при́зе̄мље is 0, so an American 5th floor is a Serbian 4th.

The door code is ши̏фра, the intercom is и̏нтерфон. In a code «*» is called звѐздица and «#» is тараба.

cyr: Relatives: стриц, ујак, теча and the rest
note:
Uncles and aunts:
• стри̑ц and стри̑на - the father's brother and his wife
• у̏ја̄к and у̏јна - the mother's brother and his wife
• те̏тка and те̏ча - a parent's sister and her husband

Nephews and nieces:
• не̏ћа̄к and не̏ћака - the general words
• се̏стрић and сестрѝчина - a sister's children
• сино̀вац and синовица - a brother's children

The husband's relatives: свѐкар, све̏крва, де̏вер, за̏ова, јѐтрва.

The wife's relatives: та̏ст, та̏шта, шу̏рак.

In practice Serbs just say «бра̏т од те́тке» or simply «брат».

related.en: hot rakija with sugar and spices

note:
The main drink is ра̀кија, a fruit brandy made from plums (шљи̏вовица), apricots, pears and quinces.

Red wine is called «црно» (black), white wine «бело».

Cocktails:
• ба̀мбус - red wine with cola, a favorite of young people
• шпри̏цер - white wine with mineral water, for older people

In winter people drink «кувано вино» (mulled wine) and «кувану ракију» with sugar and spices.

Liqueurs: медо̀вача, орахова̀ча, вишњѐвача. Бѐрмет is wine with herbs.

What is sold where:
• пи̏љарница - fruit and vegetables
• посластѝчарница - cakes and pastries
• пржионица кафе - coffee roasted on the spot
• мѐња̄чница - currency exchange
• чарапа̀ра - socks and underwear
• позаментерија - thread and sewing supplies
• кантѝна - a snack bar at a school or workplace

Бу̀тик is any small shop, the same as ду̀ћа̄н. A кинеска радња sells almost everything, and an апотека sells cosmetics and toys as well as medicines.

related.en: Nole, professor! (a fan chant about Novak Djokovic)
rip it up, go for it

note:
Addressing a man as «Професоре!» expresses approval and admiration, especially among men. People also say «ма̑јсторе», «легендо», «ца̏ре».

Fans sing «Ноле, професоре!» to Novak Djokovic.

Slang that comes from there:
• «гази!» - step on it, push forward
• «цепај!» - rip it up

cyr: Key words of the Serbian character
note:
Key words of the Serbian character:
• пола́ко - not just «slowly» but a way of life without hurry
• ѝна̄т - stubbornness for the sake of stubbornness, part of the Serbs' self-image; an angry person switches on ѝна̄т and will not give an inch
• «ма̏ло су̏тра» - «not a chance»
• a red thread on the wrist (црвени конац) guards against the evil eye, especially children and pregnant women

Children in Serbia are «little gods».

Many words of everyday life and cooking came from Turkish:
• food: ра̀кија, а̀јва̄р, ка̀јмак, ће̏вап, ћу̀фте, су̏тлија̄ш
• everyday life and character: ду̀ћа̄н, ѝна̄т
• џа̏нум - «my dear» (literally «my soul»), heard in a song by Tea Dora

If you know Turkish, these words are easy to recognize, and the other way round.

related.en: family feast of the patron saint

note:
Serbia's entries on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage:
• сла̏ва - the yearly feast of a family's patron saint
• ко̏ло - a round dance
• пе̏ва̄ње уз гу̏сле - epic poetry sung to a bowed instrument
• злакуска лончарија - pottery
• ра̀кија шљи̏вовица (since late 2022)

Крсна слава passes from father to son. In the song «Тамо далеко» the hero loses his home and «моју крсну славу».

related.en: the triumphant shout after a prank

note: April Fools' Day is «Дан шале». A successful prank ends with a triumphant «Априли-ли-ли!»

cyr: Latin without diacritics changes the meaning
note:
In songs and subtitles Serbian is often typed in «bald Latin», without š, ž, č, ć. Then different words merge:
• sisati (си̏сати) - to suck, but šišati (ши́шати) - to cut hair
• koza (ко̀за) - goat, but koža (ко̏жа) - skin

So for study it is better to use texts in Cyrillic or in full Latin.

related.en: duplex (a house for two families; a two-story apartment)
apartment with its own exit to the yard
house for two or three families

note:
A private family house is often built with several floors: the head of the family plans ahead for where his son will bring his wife.

Other types:
• гарсо̀њера - a studio apartment
• ду̏плекс - a house for two families with a shared wall, or a two-story apartment
• дворѝшни ста̑н - an apartment with an exit to the yard, more often an illegal one
• ку̏ћа на̏пола - a house for two or three families

cyr: Serbs celebrate New Year four times

related.en: Serbian New Year (the Old New Year, January 13)
family celebration of the patron saint (slava)

note:
New Year is not the main family holiday in Serbia. It is celebrated four times:
1. On the daytime of December 31 young people go out to cafes for a «дне̏вна жу̑рка».
2. At night - parties in restaurants and squares with live music (жи̏ва сви̑рка).
3. On the evening of January 1 - the «репрѝза» in bars.
4. January 13 - Ср̏пска Но̑ва го̏дина (by the Old Style calendar), often even louder.

The main family holidays are Сла̏ва, Бо̀жић and У̏скрс.

cyr: The Serbian cultural code: food and habits
note:
What Serbs like:
• ра̀кија - fruit brandy, offered to guests
• ка̀фа, Turkish style
• бу̀рек with yogurt as a snack
• ро̀штӣљ for any celebration
• Plazma biscuits as the taste of childhood
• comfortable sportswear

The music is наро̀дњаци and ту̏рбо-фо̑лк, especially at weddings.

Serbian schoolchildren chose пра̏скозо̄рје as the most beautiful word: the twilight before dawn, a symbol of hope and a new beginning.

Other favorites include ши̏шмиш, си̏јалица, шаргаре́па, кикирѝки, пара̀дајз, бомбо̀њера, ужѝвајте.

An interesting word is ра̀збибрига - any pastime, like a crossword.

cyr: The letter J is the trickiest
note:
For English speakers the trickiest letter is «Ј» (J in Latin): it is read like English «y» in «yes», not like «j» in «jam». For example Јо̀ван (Yovan), Ја̀смӣн (Yasmin), Јо̀рдан (Yordan).

Rules:
• do not mix Latin and Cyrillic in one word
• Љ and њ in Latin are Lj and Nj
• Đ is written exactly so, not «Dj»: Doviđenja (довиђе́ња), not Dovidjenja
• the word је is read «ye», as in «yes»

Рамо̀нда is a Balkan flower that looks like a violet. It revives after almost completely drying out, so it is a symbol of rebirth. Serbia's song at Eurovision 2024 was named after it.

Да̀ница is the Serbian name of Venus, the morning star, the «herald of the day». It is also a female name and a synonym of rare beauty.

In a readers' poll the least pleasant-sounding Serbian word was «ко̏пиле» (a child born out of wedlock).

Also on the list:
• ке̏ва - colloquial for mother
• ћа̏ле - colloquial for father
• пѝнђур, по̀дбрадак, гно̑ј

Many of these words are about children and parents, which shows how much Serbs value family.

cyr: Quince, the favorite fruit of Serbs
note:
Serbs especially love quince (ду̏ња): it is kept on top of the wardrobe for its scent, rakija is made from it, poems are written about it, and Ду̏ња is a girl's name.

Ма̀лина matters too: Serbia is a major exporter of raspberries, and Ма̀лина is a female name.

cyr: Lj and Nj are single sounds
note:
In Nj and Lj the letter j is not a separate «y» sound: each pair is one soft consonant, with no pause after it.

Examples:
• љу̀ља̄шка - roughly «lyoo-lya-shka», with a soft «ly» as in «million»
• њу̏шка - roughly «nyoo-shka», with «ny» as in «canyon»

Respellings are always approximate, so it is better to listen to the audio.

related.en: a stew cooked in a cauldron

note:
Labor Day (Пр̀вӣ ма̏ј, Пра̑знӣк ра̑да): May 1 and 2 are days off.

Adults go to a spa town, to other countries, or to a barbecue (ро̀штӣљ, ко̏тлић).

Young people claim spots in the forest in advance by tying ribbons to the trees, and live in tents for up to three days with loud music.

cyr: Сине! and Ћеро! - forms of address to children
note:
Parents call their children «Си̑не!» (a son or a daughter) and «Ћеро!» (a daughter only).

In congratulations and invitations the woman's name comes first.

To speak about a person's qualities, «о̏соба» is better, because «чо̏век» often means «man».

Serbs write and pronounce English names with «в» (v) in place of W:
• Ро̑н Ви̏зли, Вѝлијам Ше̏кспир, Ви̏нстон Че̏рчил
• Во̑лт Ди̏зни, Бру̑с Ви̏лис, Е̏ма Во̏тсон

The same in words: вѝкенд, Ви̏мблдон, Во̑л стри̑т.

Cartoon characters are often adapted: the Flintstones are По̀родица Кре̏менко, Huey, Dewey and Louie are Ра́ја, Га̏ја и Вла̏ја.

In Serbia relatives and close friends often drop in without calling. This is not rude: advance notice makes the hosts fuss, while a sudden visit is simply a reason to chat.

If guests did warn you a week ahead, they most likely expect a proper feast.

cyr: How to say «company party» in Serbian
note:
There is no single word for it. People say:
• жу̑рка са колѐгама
• корпора̀тивна жу̑рка
• пра̏знична жу̑рка на по̏слу
• корпора̀тивна про̏слава
• the loanword ти̏мбилдинг - barbecue, bowling, paintball, a bar

A New Year company party is «новогодишња прослава са колегама».

cyr: Names of the seven dwarfs in Serbian

related.en: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

note:
«Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs» in Serbian is «Снежана и седам патуљака». Пату́љак means both a dwarf and a little person.

The dwarfs' names are made from verbs and adjectives:
• Уча (from у̀чити) - the smart one
• Љутко (from љу́тити се) - Grumpy
• Сре̏ћко (from сре̏ћан) - Happy
• Поспа́нко (from по̏спа̄н) - Sleepy
• Стидљивко (from сти́дети се) - Bashful
• Кијавко (from ки́јати) - Sneezy
• Тупко (from ту̑п) - Dopey: not an insult but an affectionate «silly»

People in Novi Sad call a guy «гари» - roughly like «dude» or «buddy».

A local pride is the «Ѝндекс» sandwich, invented in Novi Sad.

Humorous videos about the city feature a кафа̀на, a band of тамбу̀раши (tamburitza players) and the Мѝшелук district, where fans of fast driving gather.

cyr: The persimmon «каки» and a funny coincidence
note:
In Serbia persimmons are often sold as «јапа̀нска ја̏бука» (literally «Japanese apple»), with «каки» in brackets on the price tag.

A seller asking «Колѝко ка̀ки?» wants to know how many fruits you want, but parents of small children hear «how much does he poop?» (какити is baby talk for to poop).

A case where Serbian is funny quite literally.

related.en: pljeskavica (a large patty of minced meat)

note:
The Serbian «ру̏ска сала́та» is basically Olivier salad, with some differences:
• the peas are boiled, not canned
• the mayonnaise is Serbian, with a hint of mustard, and a lot of it goes in

This salad is on the table at every celebration, and it is even put into a пљѐскавица.

In other European countries the same salad is called Russian, French or beef salad.

related.en: at the top of one's voice

note:
Serbian kindergartens teach New Year songs about Father Frost (Де̏да Мра̑з): «Са̏нке Де̏да Мра̏за» and «Звончићи» (the Serbian version of Jingle Bells).

The lyrics include па̀хуља, са̏нке, и̏рва̄с, окле́вати and the phrase на са̏в гла̑с.

related.en: the custom of searching for gifts in straw
oak branch for the Christmas Eve fire

note:
On Serbian Christmas Eve (Ба̑дњи да̑н, January 6) straw (сла̏ма) is brought into the house, and coins, tangerines and sweets are hidden in it.

Children look for the gifts and peep «пи̏јӯ-пи̏јӯ» like chicks, hence the name «пи̏јука̄ње».

The custom is relaxed and has many variants: at church, at home, or by a fire with oak branches, the «ба̏дња̄к».

On Serbian signs a ban or a warning is usually expressed with a verb in the imperative:
• «Не гази траву» - keep off the grass
• «Не дирај» - do not touch
• «Не бацај ђубре» - do not litter
• «Пази» - careful, watch out
• «Чувај се пса» - beware of the dog

On doors: «Вуци» - pull, «Гурај» - push.

A «Па̏ӯк» on a parking sign means a tow truck.

related.en: to dance on the spot, to bounce in place

note:
At a concert with seats, Serbs more often stand up and dance right by their seats, without going out into the aisle. This bouncing in one place is called «ђу̏скање».

Even in clubs there is no separate dance floor: guests stand by their sofas and tall round tables.

Lively fun is a sign of respect for the hosts, and it is rather the one who sits that gets judged.

related.en: decorating the guests at a wedding

note:
The first thing that awaits a guest at a wedding restaurant is ки̏ће̄ње (literally «decorating»).

At the entrance stand two baskets with decorations, for men and for women. The guest is given a bracelet or a pin for the chest and puts money into another basket in return - usually a few hundred or a couple of thousand dinars.

cyr: Serbian treats: Miroč cheese and chestnut puree
note:
On the menu look for «то̏пла̄ прѐдјела» (hot appetizers): they serve grilled Miroč cheese from Mount Miroč in Eastern Serbia. It squeaks on the teeth, hence the folk name «шкри̏павац».

A sweet classic is ке̏сте̄н-пи̏ре, a dessert of chestnut puree with sugar, rum and milk, topped with whipped cream.

In bakeries get a crunchy пѐреца.

The word цр̑н has many shades in Serbian:
• црно вино - red wine
• цр̑нӣ лу̏к - a common cooking onion
• поцр̀нети - to get a tan
• цр̑нӣ да̑ни - hard times
• црне паре - tainted money

In the expression «цр̑нӣ ђа̏во̄» it makes a curse stronger.

A literal translation is often wrong.

Numbers:
• police (полѝција) - 192
• fire service - 193
• ambulance - 194
• roadside assistance (А̏МСС) - 1987

Useful words: хи̏тно је, по̏жа̄р, у по̏мо̄ћ, па̏зите, ѝзгубљен сам.

Many countries are named with the feminine form of an adjective: Фра̀нцӯска̄, Нѐмачка̄, Ма̏ђарска̄, Ѐнгле̄ска̄, Шве̏дска̄ (literally «the French (land)», «the German (land)» and so on).

Some names are not what you would expect:
• Ма̏ђарска̄ - Hungary
• Нѐмачка̄ - Germany
• Уједѝњено Кра́љевство - the United Kingdom
• СА̑Д - the USA

related.en: The fish is gnawing at the fish's tail

related.sr: Четири чавчића на чунчићу чучећи цијучу
related.en: Four little jackdaws crouching on a little boat are chirping
related.acc: Чѐтири чавчѝћа на чу̏нчићу чу́че̄ћи ци̏јучу

related.en: Petar is weaving a fence for Petar

note:
A classic tongue twister: «Риба риби гризе реп».

To practice the sounds «ћ», «ч» and «ц»: «Четири чавчића на чунчићу чучећи цијучу». For «р» and «ј», «Петар Петру плете плот» is good.

cyr: Signs in the street and in the building
note:
For doors: «Вуци» - pull, «Гурај» - push.

Warnings: «Не дирај», «Не гази траву», «Не бацај ђубре», «Тишѝна».

On fences: «Чувај се пса». In a parking area: «Забрањено паркирање».

Most inscriptions use the imperative in the informal «ти» form.

«Љ» and «њ» are ligatures made of «л» and «н» with a soft sign. The letter «џ» came from Romanian Cyrillic.

These letters exist only in the Serbian alphabet (and some related ones): they stand for sounds that are spelled lj (like «lli» in «million»), nj (like «ny» in «canyon») and dž (like «j» in «jam») in Latin.

Examples: љу́бав, њѐгов, џе̏п.

cyr: What shops and places are called on signs
note:
The name of a place is often made from the goods plus the suffix -ара: мѐсара, пѝљара, књѝжара, пѐкара. There is also мѐња̄чница.

Other signs:
• печѐњара - a place selling roast meat
• посластѝчарница - a pastry shop
• амбула̀нта - a health clinic
• вулканѝзер - a tire repair shop
• ро̏бна ку̏ћа - a department store
• бензѝнска пу̑мпа - a gas station

English has only «you», but Serbian distinguishes the informal «ти» from the formal «ви̑». Serbs switch to «ти» quickly: young people, sellers and waiters often say «ти» right away.

If the formal form bothers you, you can say «немој да ми персираш». Перси́рати means to address someone with «ви».

Politeness is shown by tone and by words like мо̏лим and изво̀лите.

Serbian has two equal alphabets: Cyrillic (ћирѝлица) and Latin (латѝница). Cyrillic is the official script of the state, but signs, packaging and social media often use Latin.

Almost every Serb reads both fluently. The correspondence is one to one: љ - lj, њ - nj, џ - dž.

In everyday speech:
• руска салата - Russian salad (Olivier)
• руска зима - very severe cold
• ру̏скӣ фи̏лм - a hard, tragic story

These are humorous images, not political statements.

Жу́па is a Slavic word for a settled territory among hills and valleys. Жу̀пан is the medieval title of a regional ruler, and вѐликӣ жу̀пан is the supreme prince.

In Croatia and Hungary a жупа̀нија is an administrative unit; in Serbia the closest modern equivalent is the сре̑з.

The word appears in place names: Жу́па Александро̀вачка, Среда̀чка жу́па.

More than five centuries next to the Ottoman Empire left many Turkish loanwords:
• household: јо̀рган, ћѝлим, ме̏рдевине, со̀ка̄к, ћорсо̀ка̄к
• food: са̀рма, бу̀рек, бакла̀ва, ће̏вап
• people and relations: ко̀мшија, комшѝлук, ду̏шманин, о̀рта̄к

They sound lively and colloquial.

In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić simplified Serbian Cyrillic:
• he kept 24 of the old letters
• he added «ј», «љ», «њ», «ћ», «ђ», «џ»
• he dropped the superfluous ones (such as «ѣ»)

The principle: write as you hear, read as it is written. This brought the written language closer to the speech of the people.

related.en: to be stubborn out of spite

related.sr: он неће да пише латиницом, он је србенда
related.en: he refuses to write in Latin script, he is a србенда
related.acc: о̑н не̏ће да пи̑ше̄ латѝницом, о̑н је ср̀бе̄нда

note:
Ѝна̄т is stubbornness out of spite, even to one's own harm. Of a person one may say «у ње̏му је ѝна̄т» (he has inat in him).

The humorous «ср̀бе̄нда» means a super-patriot: «он неће да пише латиницом, он је србенда» (he won't write in Latin script, he is a србенда).

It is customary to bring a gift when visiting Serbs:
• for the hostess (дома̀ћица) - flowers or sweets
• for the host (дома̀ћин) - a bottle of rakija (ра̀кија) or wine
• for children - chocolate

The hosts will first protest that you should not have - answer «Ма̏ ка̀квӣ, нѝје то̑ ни̏шта».

You are expected to eat a lot: «Је̏ди, ни̏шта не је̏де̄ш!»

Offering to help in the kitchen is good manners. It is better to stay away from politics.

cyr: What is customary to give as a gift in Serbia
note:
The most typical gift is coffee (ка̀фа), about 200 grams: 100 is too little, more looks like showing off.

What to give to whom:
• often - chocolate and a бомбо̀њера
• to women - flowers
• to men - a bottle of rakija or wine
• to children - sweets or fruit
• to the elderly - coffee and ра́тлук

cyr: How to order coffee in Serbia
note:
Домаћа кафа is Turkish coffee made in a džezva, the most common order.

Young people often drink нес кафа (instant coffee), топли нес or хладни нес, and espresso:
• кра̀ткӣ - short
• ду̏плӣ - double
• продужени - with added water
• еспресо са млеком - espresso with milk

Simply saying «Једну кафу, молим» or «Ја ћу домаћу» is perfectly normal.

The most common is шљи̏вовица, made from plums.

Other kinds:
• комо̀вица - from grape pomace, also drunk as a medicine
• лозова̀ча - straight from grapes, popular in Montenegro
• кајсијѐвача - from apricots
• дуњева̀ча - from quince
• ви̏љамовка - from pears
• трава̀рица - plum brandy with herbs
• клеко̀вача - with juniper

Among the liqueurs: медо̀вача, орахова̀ча, вишњѐвача.

cyr: Veal, young beef and beef: телетина, јунетина, говедина
note:
Serbia distinguishes three kinds of beef:
• тѐлетина - veal, a calf under a year old, light tender meat
• јунѐтина - young cattle of 12-24 months, redder meat
• го̀ведина - from cattle older than two years, dark red, with richer fat

cyr: Summer by the calendar: when it starts
note:
For Serbs summer begins on the day of the summer solstice (about June 21) and lasts until the September equinox. Spring begins around March 20.

Congratulating someone on the first day of summer on June 1 would seem odd.

Ле̏то is the season of vacations and school holidays, but же̏га wears out pensioners.

Wedding customs:
• in front of the procession walks the барја̀кта̄р with a flag
• the groom shoots at an apple on a branch at the bride's house
• ку̑м and ку́ма are the witnesses, often later the godparents
• after the church the кум throws coins to the crowd
• at the feast the bride's shoe is «stolen» and returned for a ransom
• before the church the bride lifts a baby for the sake of future children

Бре̏ strengthens a phrase and adds emotion: surprise, irritation, joy. It is not a swear word and not an exact equivalent of «dude» or «damn». It suits friends and family, but not your boss.

Examples:
• «Ма бежи, бре!» - Oh, come off it!
• «Шта̏ је, бре̏, о̀во̄?» - What on earth is this?

The word exists in Greek and Turkish too.

related.en: You are missing one more paper

note:
Ша̀лтерка is a humorous word for a female clerk at a counter (ша̀лтер) who handles bureaucratic matters.

The meme: whatever you bring, she will say «Фали ти један папир» (you are missing one more paper), abbreviated FT1P.

The base is the grill (ро̀штӣљ): a пљѐскавица (a large patty, often stuffed with cheese and ham) and ћева̀пи.

You choose the toppings yourself, usually at no extra charge: ку̀пус сала́та, кра̏ставац, пара̀дајз, ка̀јмак, у̏рнебе̄с.

You can say «Све̏ по̀мало» (a bit of everything). To take it away: «за по̀нети».

Serbian superstitions:
• «Жѝвели» is not said with water or juice - it brings trouble
• you must not whistle in the house, you will attract mice
• a bag is not put on the floor: you will lose money
• bread must not be put upside down
• an itchy right palm means spending, the left one means money
• when clinking glasses, you look the person in the eye

Some sounds differ from English:
• duck - ква-ква
• frog - кре-кре
• piglet - гро-гро or скви-скви
• hen - ко-ко-да
• mouse - циу-циу
• pigeon - гу-гу-гу

Close to English: ав-ав (woof), мјау (meow), му-му (moo).

A cat is called with «мац-мац», like English «kitty-kitty».

related.en: like a Russian vehicle (said of something that eats up a lot of money)

note:
More «руски» in Serbian jokes:
• ру̏скӣ те̏нк - a very big person
• руски лекари - mysterious experts everyone talks about
• ру̏скӣ тра̏ктор - something that never breaks
• ру̏скӣ во̀лети - to love unconditionally
• ко руско возило - to spend a lot of money

Serbs often take their pets to cafes, restaurants and shopping malls. You may see a «pet friendly» sign on the door.

Popular breeds: Staffordshire, spitz, husky, retriever, French bulldog.

Words: ку̏ћнӣ љуби́мац - pet, па̏с - dog, ма̏чка - cat.

related.en: white bee, the most distant ancestor

note:
Serbian has separate words for ancestors many generations back: пра̀деда, чукундѐда (great-great-grandfather), наврдеда and so on.

By tradition the list goes up to the 16th generation, where «бе̑лӣ о̀рао» and «бела пчела» stand. The eagle stands for strength and immortality, the bee for a swarm of descendants.

In everyday speech only the first two or three generations are used.

Serbs switch to «ти» quickly, even with strangers, and do not find it rude. There are no patronymics.

Formal address is «госпо̀дине» / «госпођо» / «госпођице» plus the surname in the vocative. If you do not know the surname, «госпо̀дине» alone is enough.

The politest way to start a letter: «Пошто̏ванӣ» / «Поштована».

Serbian has words in which «р» is the syllable carrier: кр̑в, смр̏т, цр̑в, вр̏т, вр̏х, кр̏ст, гр̑б, тр̏г, бр̑з, пр̏ст, тр̑н, р̏т.

There is no vowel in them, but «р» forms the syllable, and the stress falls on it.

Examples:
• кр̑в - blood
• цр̑в - worm
• пр̏ст - finger
• вр̏х - top

Basic commands:
• «Седи!» - sit
• «Ста̏ни!» - stand
• «Дођи!» - come here
• «Чекај!» - wait
• «Пу̑стӣ!» - drop it
• «Ти̏хо!» - quiet

What you say to an owner: «Ка̀ка̄в фи̑н па̏с!», «Мушко или женско?». What an owner may warn you: «Плаши се», «Може да уједе».

Chatting with other dog walkers is a normal thing in Serbia.

Color adjectives in Serbian sometimes behave unexpectedly:
• пла̑ва ко̀са - blond hair (literally «blue hair»)
• цр̑нӣ лу̏к - onion (literally «black onion»)
• бе̑лӣ лу̏к - garlic (literally «white onion»)
• црно вино - red wine (literally «black wine»)
• слатка вода - fresh water (literally «sweet water»)
• кисела вода - sparkling water (literally «sour water»)

These pairs are best learned as set expressions.

related.en: coffee brought to a boil three times

note:
Serbs like to joke about themselves:
• српска посла - sloppy work and pulling strings
• ср̏пскӣ ѝна̄т - stubbornness out of spite
• српска кафа - coffee brought to a boil three times
• српска Нова година - January 13-14, by the old calendar

These are self-ironic expressions you often hear in conversation and on social media.

cyr: Serbian and Croatian: the main differences
note:
The main difference: ekavian (in Serbia: вре́ме) and ijekavian (in Croatia: вријеме).

Other differences:
• after modal verbs a Serb uses «да + present»: хоћу да радим; a Croat more often takes the infinitive: хоћу радити
• future: радићу (Serbian) and радит ћу (Croatian)
• vocabulary: па̑сош - путовница, аеро̀дром - зрачна лука, хи̏љада - тисућа

From the Turks came everyday words: џе̏п, шѐћер, ба́дем, па̀мук, јо̀рган, ка̀пија, то́рба, ча̀рапа, па̏ра, ме̏рмер, ђу̏бре, сѝрће, па̀пуча, ћо̀шак, ха̀јде.

Many of them became basic words and are not felt as loanwords.

Serbs use ха̀јде all the time, for «come on» or «let's».

cyr: A contest for a beautiful new word
note:
The website «Mala biblioteka» announced a contest for the best Serbian replacements for foreign words. The winner was «духоклонуће» instead of «депрѐсија», followed by «прохујак» (flashback) and «прикачица» (attachment).

Among the other entries:
• нежељак - spam
