• дубоклажа - deepfake
• утицајац - influencer
• промајник - air conditioner

Most of the words are still jokes and have not entered everyday use.

The word «ва̀мпӣр» is considered one of the best-known Serbian words in other languages. It spread after the case of Пѐтар Благо́јевић from the village of Кисиљево around 1725: after his death, villagers were said to have started dying suddenly.

An Austrian official described the case in a report, and a fashion for vampires swept across Europe. That is how the word got into many languages.

cyr: How to go to a Slava

related.en: family feast of the patron saint

note:
Сла̏ва is a family feast in honor of the family's patron saint. It is on the UNESCO intangible heritage list.

How to go to a Slava:
• come to the hosts hungry
• bring a symbolic gift: wine, coffee, sweets or flowers
• say «Срећна слава!» to the hosts

A Slava can be посна (fasting) or мрсна (non-fasting); on the table there is usually жи̏то and a славски колач.

The main rule of Serbian spelling: write as you speak and read as it is written.

What it means:
• each letter is always read the same way
• there are no silent letters, as there are in English
• knowing the alphabet lets you read any word at once

Ч and Ћ are different sounds: Ч is hard, Ћ is soft.

In Serbia a death is traditionally announced through читуље: obituary notices in newspapers, on poles and at building entrances.

They give the name, the dates of life, a photo and condolences (са̀учешће) from relatives. One person often gets several чѝтуља from different loved ones, so their number is sometimes taken as a measure of influence.

That is how acquaintances learn about a death and come to pay their respects.

related.en: to wait for a long time

note:
Montenegrin became official after the 2007 Constitution. Its alphabet has two more letters than the Serbian one: ś and ź (in Cyrillic «с́» and «з́»).

The pronunciation is ijekavian; in Serbia it is ekavian.

In the coastal towns Italianisms are noticeable:
• пја̏т - plate
• ленцун - bed sheet
• ду̀рати - to last

Old words:
• че̏ља̄д - people
• ба̀нути - to turn up suddenly
• дре̏ждати - to wait, long and in vain

related.en: Serbian bogeywoman, sister of Baba Yaga
beauty of the mountains and waters

note:
Serbian fairy-tale and mythical beings:
• Баба Рога - the Serbian sister of Baba Yaga: an old woman with a horn who frightens children
• Ба̏ш Чѐлик - a villain like Koschei: his death is hidden in a bird or an animal
• Ала - a demon that swallows the sun and moon during an eclipse; people scared it away with noise
• Ви́ла - a beauty of the mountains and waters
• Мо̏ра - a nightmare spirit that chokes sleepers
• Некрштеници - restless souls of unborn and unbaptized children

related.en: to tap eggs against each other

note:
Easter in Serbia is celebrated for three days.

Egg customs:
• eggs are dyed (фарбати јаја) with onion skins (ко̏ра од лу́ка)
• the very first egg is red; it is called чува̀ркућа and stays in the house until next Easter; red stands for life
• people crack eggs against each other (куцати се јајима): whoever's egg does not break wins and takes the other egg
• guests bring one egg for each member of the host's household

related.sr: Горе горе горе горе, нег' што доле горе горе.
related.en: Up there the forests burn worse than down here.
related.acc: Го̏ре го̏ре го̏ре го̏ре, не̏г' што̏ до̏ле го̏ре го̏ре.

note:
A word game: «Горе горе горе горе, нег' што доле горе горе».

Words that sound the same:
• го̏ре - up, above
• го̏ре - worse
• го̏ре - (they) burn
• го̏ре - forests (pl. of гора)

The phrase means: up there the forests burn worse than down below. It shows how many homonyms Serbian has.

February 15 is Serbia's Дан државности. It is tied to two events:
• 1804 - in the village of Orašac it was decided to start the First Serbian Uprising (у̀станак)
• 1835 - on the feast of Сретење the first constitution was adopted in Kragujevac (Сретењски устав)

So the holiday is also a Constitution Day (у̏ста̄в).

Ex-YU rock is the rock music (ро̏к) that developed in the former Yugoslavia (бивша Југославија).

In the 1970s and 80s the scene was vibrant, and musicians from Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia shared fans.

Legendary bands (гру̏па):
• Бијело дугме
• Азра
• Елѐктричнӣ орга̀зам
• Рибља чорба
• Идоли

The songs live on after the breakup of the country.

To show affection for things and people, a suffix is added to the word:
• feminine nouns more often take -ица: ку̏ћа - ку̏ћица, ма̏чка - ма̏чкица
• masculine nouns take -ић: гра̑д - градић

But Serbian uses diminutives less than you might expect: instead of «little eyebrows, little nails» people just say о̏брве, но̏кти.

Men's costume: a шајка̀ча, a white shirt, a dark пр̀слук, wide trousers, чара̀пе and leather опа̀нци with straps.

Women wore long embroidered shirts and a vest called тлек; belts were an important part.

Patterns can be floral, geometric or charms against evil. In Vojvodina the embroidery is richer, in the south the clothing is simpler. Today the costume is worn on holidays.

In Serbia films and cartoons are shown in the original language with Serbian subtitles (тѝтл, pl. титлови), not dubbed.

That makes it easy to practice listening and reading at once, both at the cinema and at home.

In Serbia eggs are dyed on Вѐликӣ пе́так (Good Friday).

The first egg is red and is called чува̀ркућа: it is kept at home, and people believe it protects the house and the family all year.

On Easter Day people play куцање јајима: everyone takes an egg and taps it against an opponent's egg. The one whose egg stays whole wins.

Titles and character names of cartoons in Serbia often differ from the English ones:
• Donald Duck - Паја Патак
• Bugs Bunny - Душко Дугоушко
• Smurfs - Штрумпфови
• Minions - Малци
• «Lady and the Tramp» - Маза и Луња
• «Cinderella» - Пепѐљуга
• «The Ugly Duckling» - Ру̑жно па̏че

Learn the terms along with familiar stories: they stick better that way.

cyr: Burek: with meat or with cheese

related.en: in Serbia a layered pie, in Bosnia only with meat

note:
In Serbia бу̀рек is a layered pie, and «бурек са сиром» is perfectly normal.

In Bosnia «бурек» means only the one with meat. Other pies are called differently:
• with cheese - си́рница
• with potatoes - кромпируша
• with spinach - зељаница
• general name - пи̏та

So in Bosnia ordering «бурек са сиром» will cause surprise.

The Serbian ћирилица has 30 letters, and each stands for one sound. The principle of writing: «write as you speak, read as it is written».

Separate sounds got their own letters: «ј», «љ», «њ», «ћ», «ђ», «џ».

That is why there are no silent letters in it.

related.en: family feast of the patron saint

note:
Serbs jokingly call January све̑тӣ ја̏нуа̄р: one holiday follows another.

• Christmas (Бо̀жић)
• Све̑тӣ Сте̏фа̄н
• the Serbian New Year (by the Julian calendar)
• the сла̏ва of Saint Sava at the end of the month

People work reluctantly at this time and switch to «супер полако» mode.

related.en: wife of one's husband's brother; wives of two brothers

note:
Serbian has many precise words for relatives, which can seem unnecessary to an English speaker:
• uncles - стри̑ц (father's brother) and у̏ја̄к (mother's brother)
• aunt - те̏тка, one word for both the father's and the mother's sister
• uncles' wives - стри̑на and у̏јна
• wives of two brothers - јетрве
• husband's sister - за̏ова

A separate topic is ку́мство: godparents and ку̏мови are considered close family, and such ties are highly valued in the village.

cyr: What the end piece of a loaf is called
note:
The end piece of a loaf has different names in Serbia, depending on the region:
• окра̏јак
• крајка
• пупушка - in Vojvodina
• попак, рубак, ка̀нтӯн - in some other places

There is a joking belief about this piece: whoever likes it will get a good mother-in-law.

cyr: Полако as a way of life

related.en: I'm living at an easy pace.
tavern, place for food and drink

note:
Пола́ко is not only «slowly». It also means «take it easy, don't take it to heart».

The word has become almost a motto of Serbian unhurriedness:
• an answer to Ка̏ко си? - «I'm living easy»
• attitude to time: па̑р го̏дина can mean four to six years
• attitude to money: small change is not counted, and friends treat each other in the кафана

If you write Serbian in the Latin alphabet without š, č, ć, ž, đ, the meaning can change:
• šiške (bangs) and siske are different words
• šišanje (haircut) and sisanje (sucking)
• kuća (house) turns into kuca (little dog, bitch)

So it is better to use the diacritics or to write in Cyrillic.

related.en: name of a village or mountain
name of a village or mountain
name of a village or mountain
name of a village or mountain

note:
Serbia has villages and mountains whose names make people smile:
• Мокре Гаће
• Смрључ
• Прљуша
• Курило
• Орал

Locals are not bothered by them, and for tourists they become a reason for a photo by the road sign.

Besides the usual ја̏нуа̄р, фе̏бруа̄р and so on, there are folk month names based on natural signs:
• сечањ - January
• вѐљача - February
• тра̑вањ - April
• цветањ - May
• ср̑пањ - July or August
• гро̏здобер - grape harvest time
• ли̏стопа̄д - autumn

The names differ by region and are almost never heard in speech.

related.en: to drink Šumadija tea - to go for a rakija

note:
Шумадијски чај is not tea but a hot drink made from шљивовица or another rakija with sugar, water and, if you like, honey. It is drunk in winter in company, to warm up.

If you hear пити шумадијски чај, you are being invited for a rakija, not for herbal tea.

related.sr: Да ли је аутомобил полован или нов?
related.en: Is the car used or new?
related.acc: Да ли је аутомо̀бӣл по̀лован и̏ли но̏в?

related.sr: Да ли је могућа пробна вожња?
related.acc: Да ли је мо̀гућа про̏бна во̀жња?

related.en: Has the car been in an accident?

related.sr: Да ли је могуће платити на рате?
related.en: Is it possible to pay in installments?
related.acc: Да ли је мо̏гӯће пла́тити на ра̏те?

related.en: When was the technical inspection done?
Can you show me the service book?

note:
Useful questions for the seller:
• Да ли је аутомо̀бӣл по̀лован и̏ли но̏в?
• Колика је километража?
• Да ли је могућа пробна вожња?
• Да ли је аутомобил ударан? - that is, has it been in an accident
• Да ли је мо̏гӯће пла́тити на ра̏те?
• Када је рађен технички преглед?
• Можете ли показати сервисну књижицу?

related.en: What are you doing, you silly donkey?

note:
Serbian often insults people with animal names:
• ма̀гарац - a fool or a stubborn person
• сви́ња - a slob or a miser
• кра̏ва - a slow person
• змѝја - a treacherous person
• о́вца - someone who blindly follows the crowd

It usually sounds grumbling and playful: Шта радиш, магарче један?

Serbian has phrases that read the same from left to right and from right to left:
• Ана воли Милована
• Сир има мирис
• Ања себе сања
• Маче једе јечам
• Они воле вело вино

The word «палиндром» is hardly found in textbooks, but this is good practice for reading and vocabulary.

New Year: је̏лка, ку́гла, паху̀љица, ва̏троме̄т, Де̏да Мра̏з.

Christmas: Бо̀жић, Бадње вече, а̑нђео, све́ћа, вѐнчић.

Greetings:
• Срећна Нова година!
• Сре̏ћан Бо̀жић!
• at Christmas - Христос се роди! and in reply Ваистину се роди!

Шопска салата is a salad of tomatoes (пара̀дајз), cucumbers (кра̏ставац), sweet peppers and onions with white brined cheese (си̏р) and oil.

The Shopi are an ethnic group at the meeting point of Serbia, Bulgaria and North Macedonia. The salad has become a symbol of the Balkans, and the name took hold in tourist restaurants in Bulgaria in the 1950s.

Serbian Бо̀жић falls on January 7, by the Julian calendar.

On Christmas Eve (Бадњи дан) a ба̏дња̄к - an oak branch - is brought into the house and burned in the stove.

At the Christmas lunch the family shares the чесница, a round bread with a coin. Whoever gets the coin will have good luck all year.

People greet each other like this: Христос се роди! - Ваистину се роди!

related.en: coffee in the morning to wake up
coffee for a long chat with friends

note:
Serbs have jokey names for coffee depending on the occasion:
• раздремуша - in the morning, to wake up
• дочекуша - for a long-awaited guest
• разговоруша - for a long chat with friends

The words are formed on the pattern «action + -уша». The humor is colloquial and not for the dictionary.

cyr: How to dictate an e-mail address
note:
How to dictate an address:
• @ - ет; in conversation there is also ма̀јмунче («little monkey»), but it is not used in business speech
• dot - та̏чка
• hyphen - цр̏тица
• underscore - доња црта

First you specify: све малим словима («all in lowercase»).

Example: ма̑рко доња црта де̏вет јѐдан ет џи мејл та̏чка ком

Serbian wedding vocabulary:
• запро̀сити дѐво̄јку - to propose
• вѐридба - engagement
• мла̑да and младо̀жења - bride and groom
• младѐнци - newlyweds
• венча̀ница - wedding dress
• ве̏о - veil
• по́зӣвница - invitation

Guests usually arrive late - all in the spirit of пола́ко.

cyr: Latin script without diacritics: сисање or шишање?
note:
On social media Serbs often write in the Latin alphabet without č, ć, š, ž, đ, and the meaning changes:
• sisati - to suck, šišati - to cut hair
• sarma - stuffed cabbage rolls, šarm - charm
• kuca - little dog, kuća - house
• kolac - stake, kolač - cake
• strasno - passionately, strašno - terrible

Look at the context.

The Shopi are a group living at the meeting point of Serbia, Bulgaria and North Macedonia, hence the name.

The modern salad was invented in the 1950s for tourists in Bulgaria. It has tomatoes (пара̀дајз), cucumbers (кра̏ставац), pepper, onion, white cheese (бе̑лӣ си̏р) and oil.

Today шопска салата is a dish that symbolizes the whole Balkans.

Some Serbs subconsciously believe in the power of words and avoid the dangerous name.

A snake is called непоменица (better not to mention it) or она отровна.

A cancer diagnosis is called најгора болест or она болест.

cyr: The language of Serbian real estate ads
note:
In ads for houses for sale it pays to read between the lines:
• прилика за улагање - often a house to be demolished
• топли дом - a run-down building with a stove
• аутентична кућа - an old house untouched by renovation
• потребна мања адаптација - something more serious than cosmetic work
• легализација у току - a building that is not officially registered

related.en: рога, a variety of flat red pepper
капија, a variety of red pepper

note:
Real Serbian а̀јва̄р is made from roasted red peppers of the рога or ка̀пија varieties: flat, fleshy, dark red.

How it is made:
1. Roast the peppers over a fire or in the oven.
2. Steam them under a lid.
3. Peel and grind them.
4. Cook them down for a long time in oil.

The Macedonian version adds патлѝџа̄н (eggplant), and a mix with hot pepper and garlic is called љутѐница.

It is better not to call the pepper «Bulgarian» in front of a Serb.

cyr: The cucumber and the toad are relatives
note:
Кра̏ставац (cucumber) and кра̀стача (toad) come from кра̏ста - a crust, a scab. Both the cucumber and the toad are covered with bumpy skin.

Do not mix up the words: жа̏ба is a frog, and a toad is кра̀стача.

cyr: Feminine words used only in the plural
note:
Some Serbian words are used only in the plural but are feminine. Many of them name one object made of two parts:
• ма̀казе - scissors
• пантало́не - trousers
• фа̀рмерке - jeans
• но̀вине - newspaper
• сао̀нице - sled
• бо̀гиње - smallpox
• жму̏рке - blind man's buff

The rare бука̀гије (shackles) and чезе (a light carriage) are the same.

The suffix -џија came from Turkish and denotes a person's trade or inclination:
• ћевабџија - a seller of ćevapi
• шешѝрџија - a hatter
• ча̀мџија - a boatman
• кују̀нџија - an obsolete word, today people say зла̀та̄р

The words галамџија (loudmouth), ларамџија (troublemaker) and силѐџија (hooligan) are formed the same way.

cyr: The pumpkin in the Serbian language and idioms

related.en: to be in cahoots, to act together
to fool someone, to play a prank on someone
literally: a pumpkin without a root

note:
In Serbian the pumpkin is called ти̏ква or бу̀ндева. There are also regional variants: бу̏ча, вр̏г (bottle gourd), лудаја, мисирача, дулек.

Many idioms:
• покондирена тиква
• пукла тиква
• дувати у исту тикву
• садити тикве с неким
• тиква без корена

Words that are used only in the plural still have a gender in Serbian.

Feminine classics:
• пантало́не
• ма̀казе
• но̀вине

Rarer ones:
• хулахо̀пке, га̏ће, стѐпенице, ме̏рдевине
• ја̏сле, са̏нке, гу̏сле, ви̏ле
• рашље, рачве, гру̑ди
• бо̀гиње, жму̏рке, фина̀нсије

Although Serbs follow Vuk's rule "write as you speak", mistakes happen.

Written together instead of separately:
• «самном» instead of са мно̑м
• «неможу» instead of не мо̀гу
• «видеће те» instead of ви̏дећете

Common mistakes inside words:
• «сумљам» instead of сумњам - dissimilation
• «прекључе» instead of пре̏кјуче̄ - an inserted л
• «хвали» instead of фали - hypercorrection
• «предпоставља» instead of претпоставља

The mistake «ми бих чули» instead of ми бисмо чули: the auxiliary verb changes by person.

Serbian dislikes two vowels in a row, so an extra «ј» appears: «авијон» instead of авѝо̄н.

«Требамо да» is a Croatianism; in Serbian you say требало би да.

cyr: The Niš dialect: cases fade away
note:
In the Niš dialect the cases are gradually being lost under the influence of neighboring languages, and prepositions make the endings redundant.

So the instrumental and the locative are replaced by the accusative: «са књигу» instead of са књигом.

related.en: rich dough (enriched with eggs and butter)
plain unleavened dough (stretched, as for strudel)

note:
Serbian names of dough:
• дизано - yeast dough
• кисело - rich dough
• бѝсквӣт - sponge, biscuit
• ливено - batter, for pancakes
• лиснато - puff pastry
• водено or вучено - plain, unleavened
• прхко - shortcrust
• принцес маса - choux pastry, for eclairs
• и̏нтегра̄лно - wholegrain
• смрзнуто - frozen

In Serbian ко̑т means a litter, a brood, and also a breed.

Hence окотити се - to give birth to young (of various animals, a panda among them).

A male cat is ма́чак, while ма̏чка came from Hungarian.

related.en: mule (offspring of a donkey stallion and a mare)
hinny (offspring of a stallion and a female donkey)

note:
Horse colors:
• вра́нац - black
• бе́лац, чѝла̄ш - white
• си́вац, зѐле̄нко - gray
• дорат - bay
• а̀ла̄т, риђан - chestnut
• кулаш - dun
• шарац - piebald

More words:
• ко̀била - mare, ждре̑бе - foal
• мула - mule (donkey and mare)
• ма̀зга - hinny (horse and female donkey)

related.en: fight fire with fire (literally: a nail is driven out by a nail)

note:
Many Latin proverbs have Serbian counterparts:
• manus manum lavat - рука руку мије
• divide et impera - завади па владај
• clavus clavo - клин се клином избија
• per aspera ad astra - кроз тр̑ње до зве́зда

cyr: Stress: Kruševac and the Neo-Shtokavian shift
note:
In standard Serbian the stress moved one syllable forward in the 15th-16th centuries: рукА, ногА became рУка, нОга. Below, the stressed syllable is written with a capital letter.

In Old Shtokavian dialects, for example that of Kruševac, the stress stayed where it was before the shift:
• палАчинке, not палачИнке
• бАнана, not банАна
• нУтела, not нутЕла

This is a dialect, not the standard: nobody talks like that on TV.

Пољопрѝвреда is divided into branches:
• воћарство - fruit growing
• рата́рство - field crops
• повртарство - vegetable growing
• сточа́рство - livestock

Земљора́дња is farming, and пољопри̏вредник and земљо̀ра̄днӣк both mean a farmer.

Бѐрба is the harvest, picking; the verb is бра̏ти.

Relief and geography:
• клѝсура - a gorge with gentle slopes
• лѝтица - with steep slopes
• окопина - grotto
• пѐћина - cave
• ма̏јдан - a small quarry or mine
• прераст - natural stone bridge
• сига - tufa
• слив реке - river basin

cyr: Names of plants: хајдучка трава and посекотина
note:
Хајдучка трава is yarrow, from ха̀јдӯк (an outlaw).

Посеко̀тина is St John's wort, and in everyday speech a cut: the word is used both for the herb and for the wound.

These are folk names, not scientific ones.

The root црп- means "to scoop, to draw (liquid)":
• цр̏псти, ѝсцр̄псти
• и̏сцрпан - exhaustive
• ѝсцрпљен - worn out
• исцр̀пљив, не̏исцр̄пан

Grouping words by root helps memory. The same goes for the root мор-: у́мор, о̀дмор, за̀моран.

cyr: Serbian words for a pipe and a tube
note:
Many different Serbian words where English has just "pipe" or "tube":
• ди̏мња̄к, о̀џак - chimney, flue
• лу̀ла - smoking pipe
• слу̏шалица - telephone receiver
• це̑в - water pipe
• цѐвчица - small tube
• сла̀мчица - drinking straw
• тру́ба - trumpet
• а̀успух - exhaust pipe

cyr: Beer: how people talk about it
note:
Beer is светло or тамно (light or dark), точено (draft); craft beer is занатско пиво.

Домаће пиво is beer produced locally, not homemade beer.

More words:
• пѝвара - brewery
• пи́вница - pub
• кри́гла - beer mug

What beer is made of: сла̑д (malt), хме̏љ (hops), ква́сац (yeast).

cyr: Плав and the Polovtsians; Serbian «tlat» words
note:
Пла̑в means a pale color in the range from yellow to blue, so пла̑ва ко̀са is fair hair. The name of the Polovtsians (Cumans) comes from the same root ("yellow").

Proto-Slavic tolt becomes tlat in Serbian:
• гла́ва - head
• мла̑д - young
• гла̑с - voice
• бла̏то - swamp

cyr: The Kosovo dialect: how it differs
note:
The speech of southern Kosovo and Metohija differs in these ways:
• the stress falls on other syllables: СрбИја, писАли. The stressed syllable is written with a capital letter
• there are almost no tones or lengths
• a simplified case system: the accusative merged with the locative - студирао у Београд instead of студирао у Београду

This is not a mistake, but foreigners are advised to learn the standard.

Stages of the school system:
• вр̀тић - kindergarten
• нулто одељење - the preparatory year (grade zero)
• основна школа - 8 years, lower and upper grades
• средња школа - secondary: гѝмна̄зија (academic) or стручна школа (vocational)

The year is divided into полугодишта (half-years) or тромесечја (terms). A break is ра́спуст, winter (зимски) or summer (летњи).

Foreign words in Serbian sometimes have a gender you would not guess:
• мо̑ј про̀грам, мо̑ј про̀бле̄м - masculine
• мо̀ја су̏па, мо̀ја адрѐса - feminine

The constitution is usually called у̏ста̄в, and еконо̀мија is the economy.

Serbian has no ü sound, so French ü is written with и:
• пи̏ре, жѝрӣ, мѐнӣ, би̏ро
• нија̀нса
• Цирих, Брѝсел, Мѝнхен
• Кири

Surrealism is надреалѝзам. Brochure stays брошура, not «брошира».

Nicknames in «-и» (Зоки, Боки, Паки, Мики, Ла̏кӣ) are declined, and a «ј» is inserted between «и» and the ending:
• од Пакија
• дајем Пакију
• са Пакијем
• воли Пакија
• о Пакију
• vocative - Паки!

Not declined: foreign words ending in two vowels (кака̏о), some colors and Chinese names.

cyr: Adjectives with no exact English equivalent
note:
Adjectives that have no exact English equivalent:
• па̏метан - smart, and also "knowledgeable"
• зго̏дан - with a nice figure
• опу̏штен - relaxed, at ease
• пошто̏ванӣ - respected, "dear"; you can address people this way even without a name, it is not rude
• насмѐјан - smiling, cheerful
• ша̏шав - eccentric, quirky
• за̀послен - employed
• фи̑н - nice, decent
• ки̏лав - sluggish, limp

Separately: же́дан сам - "I'm thirsty".

In Serbian, feminine forms of job titles are standard:
• лѐкарка, фри̏зерка
• мѝниста̄рка, дѝректорка
• научница

But адво̀ка̄т, инжѐње̄р, прево̀дилац, во̀за̄ч, тре́нер are traditionally masculine.

Forms such as боркиња, фотографкиња, политикологиња are considered non-standard by the language academy.

cyr: The suffix -арина: a fee for something
note:
The suffix -арина forms names of a fee or tax:
• путарѝна - road toll
• мостарина - bridge toll
• стана̀рина - rent
• школа̀рина - tuition
• члана̀рина - membership fee

Obsolete: трошарина (excise tax), крчмарина, сплаварина, свадбарина.

The stress falls on -ин-: путарИна.

cyr: Serbianization and Latinization of foreign names
note:
Serbs write foreign names as they are pronounced: По̑л (Paul), И́го (Hugo). Croats, on the contrary, keep the original.

Another trend: words like online, wi-fi and job titles stay in English, in the Latin alphabet.

The vocative does not express a relation between words, so it has no single ending:
• feminine words more often take -о (кафано)
• sometimes it coincides with the nominative
• forms differ by region

cyr: Aorist and imperfect: the fairy-tale tenses
note:
Пѐрфект is the ordinary past tense.

Two other forms are rarer:
• the aorist (from perfective verbs: ја̑ рѐкох) - an emotional retelling of quick events, or a bookish style
• the imperfect (from imperfective verbs: ја̑ бе̏х) - narration of events long ago

In speech you only need the perfect; it is enough to recognize the others when you read fairy tales.

cyr: The suffix -ина: names of sizes and measures
note:
The suffix -ина forms nouns of size from adjectives:
• ду̏г - дужѝна
• шѝрок - ширѝна
• дѐбео - дебљѝна
• гу̑ст - густѝна
• вѝсок - висѝна
• ду̀бок - дубѝна
• те́жак - тежѝна

Watch the alternation in the root: д > ж (дужѝна), ео > љ (дебљѝна).

All these words are feminine, and the question is always «колика је...?» (how big is...?).

In 2021 the Law on Gender Equality came into force in Serbia, and a guide to "родно осетљив језик" (gender-sensitive language) was issued with it.

Here the word ро̑д means social gender, and по̑л means biological sex.

The guide recommends:
• naming both groups: дру̏гови и дру̑гарице, студенти и студенткиње
• using feminine forms of job titles

The idea caused controversy: critics find such forms clumsy.

related.en: certificate of registration of a foreigner at the place of stay

note:
In Serbia a residence permit is processed at the полицијска управа (police department). Temporary residence is called прѝвременӣ бо̀равак.

The grounds are given with по основу:
• школовања - studies
• спајања породице - family reunification
• лечења - medical treatment
• власништва над непокретношћу - ownership of real estate

Бе̑лӣ ка̀рто̄н is a certificate of registration of a foreigner at the place of stay.

Many words are built from the root клиз- ("to slide"):
• кли̏зав (slippery), кли́зити (to slide)
• кли̏зӣште (landslide)
• клѝзалӣште (skating rink)
• клѝзаљке (ice skates)
• клѝза̄ч (skater)
• уметничко клизање (figure skating)

Sliding doors and sliding wardrobes also "slide": клизна врата, клизни орман.

Sea fish: орада (bream), бранцин (sea bass), ту̏на, ха̀рӣнга (herring), бака̀ла̄р (cod), о̏слић (hake).

River fish: ша̀ран (carp), гр̀ге̄ч (perch), сму̑ђ (pikeperch), со̏м (catfish).

Seafood is мо̀рскӣ пло̀дови or пло̀дови мо̏ра:
• лѝгње (squid), шкољке (clams), да̏гње (mussels)
• ко̀зице (shrimp), о̏стрига (oyster)

related.en: the first guest on Christmas Day
to visit, to come to see

note:
Christmas Eve in Serbian is Ба̏дњи да̑н. The word is linked to the verb "to keep vigil", and there is also a folk legend about a god Badnya.

On this day people burn the ба̏дња̄к - oak branches.

Че̏сница is a ritual loaf that is broken by hand (hence ча̑ст, a share).

По̀ложајник is the first guest on Christmas Day; he brings luck to the house. The word is formed from по̀лазити.

related.sr: један плус три једнако је четири
related.acc: јѐдан плу̑с три̑ је̏дна̄ко је чѐтири

related.sr: пет минус два једнако је три
related.acc: пе̑т ми́нус два̑ је̏дна̄ко је три̑

related.sr: пет пута два једнако је десет
related.acc: пе̑т пу̏та два̑ је̏дна̄ко је де̏сет

related.sr: двадесет подељено са два једнако је десет
related.en: twenty divided by two equals ten
related.acc: два́десет подѐљено са два̑ је̏дна̄ко је де̏сет

note:
Operations:
• са̀бира̄ње (+)
• о̀дузима̄ње (-)
• мно̏же̄ње (x)
• де̏ље̄ње (:)

How examples are read:
• 1 + 3 = 4 - један плус три једнако је четири
• 5 - 2 = 3 - пет минус два једнако је три
• 5 x 2 = 10 - пет пута два једнако је десет
• 20 : 2 = 10 - двадесет подељено са два једнако је десет

Division can be са остатком or без остатка (with or without a remainder).

related.en: the apartment is in its original condition (not renovated since it was built)

note:
Listings for apartments for sale say:
• ко̀мплетно реновѝра̄ње - complete renovation
• де̏лимично реновѝра̄ње - partial
• козметички радови - cosmetic

The phrase стан је у изворном стању means the apartment has not been renovated since it was built and is in its original condition.

cyr: Setting up a company in Serbia: words

related.en: proof of payment of the fee

note:
Who is who:
• legal entity - пра̑вно ли́це
• entrepreneur (sole proprietor) - предузѐтник
• LLC - друштво са ограниченом одговорношћу (ДОО)

How to register a company with the Агенција за привредне регистре (АПР):
1. Submit a пријава.
2. State the назив фирме and the ши̏фра дела́тности.
3. Attach the доказ о плаћеној такси.

The tax regime is паушално опорезивање (flat-rate taxation). VAT is ПДВ (порез на додату вредност).

cyr: Buying a car: body type and drive

related.en: It has covered a hundred thousand kilometers.

note:
Body types:
• лимузи́на - sedan
• хе̏чбек
• кара̀ва̄н - station wagon
• терѐнац or џи̏п - SUV
• ко̏мби - minibus, van

Drive: пре̑дњӣ, за̏дњӣ or на чѐтири то̏чка (front, rear or four-wheel).

Year of manufacture is го̀диште. Mileage is described with the verb пре̑ћи: «Прешао је сто хиљада километара».

For inhabitants of countries Serbian has separate masculine and feminine words:
• Ср̏бин - Ср̏пкиња
• Ру̏с - Ру̏скиња
• Ѐнгле̄з - Ѐнглескиња
• Хр̀ва̄т - Хрватица
• Не́мац - Нѐмица
• Алба́нац - А̀лба̄нка
• Црно̀горац - Црно̀го̄рка

In the plural the masculine form is used: Срби, Ру̏си, Алба́нци.

The language is named with an adjective: ср̏пскӣ, ру̏скӣ, нѐмачкӣ, ѐнгле̄скӣ.

cyr: Titles of foreign books in Serbian

related.en: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
Love in the Time of Cholera (Márquez)

note:
Many titles of foreign books sound different from the English ones:
• О̀рка̄нскӣ ви́сови - Wuthering Heights
• Ловац у житу - The Catcher in the Rye
• Врли нови свет - Brave New World
• Животињска фарма - Animal Farm
• Госпо̀да̄р му̀ва - Lord of the Flies
• Лет изнад кукавичјег гнезда - One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
• Ја̏днӣци - Les Misérables
• Стра́нац - The Stranger
• Љубав у доба колере - Love in the Time of Cholera, by Márquez

cyr: Titles of Russian books in Serbian
note:
Russian classics are translated into Serbian close to the original, but some titles differ:
• Зло̀чин и ка̏зна - Crime and Punishment
• Зли̑ ду̏си - Demons
• Ко̏цка̄р - The Gambler
• Ра̏т и ми̑р - War and Peace
• Златно теле - The Golden Calf
• Два́нае̄ст сто̀лица - The Twelve Chairs
• Једноспратна Америка - Little Golden America
• Шта̏ да се ра̏ди? - What Is to Be Done?
• Ка̀вкаскӣ затворѐнӣк - The Prisoner of the Caucasus
• Жѝвот ѝнсека̄та̄ - The Life of Insects

Meat is named from the animal with the suffix -етина:
• сви́ња - свѝњетина (pork)
• јуне - јунѐтина (beef)
• тѐле - тѐлетина (veal)
• ја̏гње - ја̀гњетина (lamb)
• пи̏ле - пѝлетина (chicken)

There is also a descriptive form: свињско месо, јунеће месо, пилеће месо, ћуреће месо, коњско месо.

These names are on the signs at a butcher's shop.

related.sr: Ако изговориш моје име, више ме неће бити
related.en: If you say my name, I will be gone
related.acc: А̏ко изго̀вориш мо̀је и̏ме, ви̏ше̄ ме не̏ће би̏ти

related.sr: Цео свет види, а себе не види
related.en: The whole world sees, but it cannot see itself
related.acc: Це̏о све̑т ви̏ди, а се̏бе не ви̏ди

related.sr: У кућу улазиш, са мном се руковаш
related.en: You enter the house, you shake hands with me
related.acc: У ку̏ћу у̀лазиш, са мно̑м се руко̀ваш

related.sr: Баци га горе - бело, баци га доле - жуто
related.en: Throw it up - it is white, throw it down - it is yellow
related.acc: Ба̏ци га го̏ре - бѐло, ба̏ци га до̏ле - жу̏то

note:
Riddles (загонетке) are built on playing with meaning. Examples, with the answer after the dash:
• «Ако изговориш моје име, више ме неће бити» - тишѝна (silence)
• «Цео свет види, а себе не види» - о̏ко (eye)
• «У кућу улазиш, са мном се руковаш» - ква̏ка (door handle)
• «Баци га горе - бело, баци га доле - жуто» - ја́је (egg)

cyr: Titles of foreign films in Serbian

related.en: Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels

note:
Serbian titles of foreign films are often translated differently from the English ones:
• Америчка лепота - American Beauty
• Бојеви метак - Full Metal Jacket
• Две чађаве двоцевке - Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels
• Недодѝрљивӣ - The Intouchables
• Неки то воле вруће - Some Like It Hot
• Ра̏тови зве́зда - Star Wars
• Умри мушки - Die Hard

Masculine job titles are formed with suffixes:
• -ац - пи́сац, про̀да̄вац
• -лац - слу̀шалац, глѐдалац
• -ар - ме̏са̄р, ри̏ба̄р
• -ач - во̀за̄ч, пѐва̄ч
• -ник - ра̑днӣк
• -ист(а) - економиста
• -аш - коша̀рка̄ш
• -ер - фудба̀ле̄р
• -тељ - у̀читељ, во̀дитељ
• -џија - ћевапџија, a Turkish suffix for trades

Which suffix to choose cannot be derived by a rule: it simply developed that way in the language.

cyr: Feminine forms of job titles and of inhabitants
note:
Feminine forms are made like this:
• -ац, -ач, -аш > -ица: продава̀чица, воза̀чица, кошарка̀шица
• -ар, -ер > -ка: месарка, тенисерка
• -ник > -ица: радница
• -ист(а) > -киња: економисткиња
• -тељ > -ка or -ица: водитељка, учитѐљица
• -џија > -ка

Inhabitants:
• Бео̀грађанин - Бео̀грађа̄нка
• Црно̀горац - Црно̀го̄рка
• Сара̀јлија - Са̀ра̄јка
• Не́мац - Нѐмица
• Ру̏с - Ру̏скиња

related.en: The green vegetables were not tasty.

note:
Words in -је denote many objects, but grammatically they are neuter singular:
• ка̀ме̄ње, ли̑шће, пе̑рје
• во̀ће, по̀врће
• др̀ве̄ће, цве̑ће

The verb is singular, and the adjective is neuter:
• Моје цвеће је свеже.
• Зелено поврће није било укусно.
• Дрвеће је већ жуто.

Abstract nouns are formed with suffixes:
• -ота - лепо̀та, срамо̀та
• -ина - топлѝна, величѝна
• -ило - лу̀дило
• -ај - по̏куша̄ј, о̏прошта̄ј, за̏грља̄ј
• -ба - сва̀дба, вѐридба, бо̀рба
• -ња - ше́тња, па̀тња, пре́тња
• -ње - чѝта̄ње, образова́ње
• -ство - пријатѐљство
• -ост - ста̏ро̄ст, хра́бро̄ст, захва́лно̄ст

Words in -ост are always feminine.

Besides the usual surnames in -ић, Bosnia has nickname surnames. People took them under Austria-Hungary, when everyone was required to have a surname.

Many mean everyday words or traits:
• Врачар - healer
• Шѐгрт - apprentice
• Дроњак - ragamuffin
• Ђога - oaf
• Ждеро - glutton
• Га̏ће - underpants
• Копривица - little nettle

cyr: Money in Serbian: from standard to slang
note:
The neutral word is но̀вац. Cash is ке̏ш, готовѝна.

Па̏ре is colloquial, but acceptable everywhere except in documents.

Slang:
• ло́ва, ки̑нта, ди̏нџа
• шушке - paper money
• зеленбаћ - greenbacks, dollars
• денге - borrowed from Russian

Sums:
• ба̀нка - a tenner
• со̏м - a grand
• кило, ци́гла - a million

According to the Ethnographic Museum, black stands for night, death and danger, but also for modesty, melancholy and rebellion (rock culture).

Hence the expressions:
• црна овца - black sheep
• црне мисли - dark thoughts
• цр̑нӣ ху̀мор - black humor
• црна листа - blacklist
• црна рупа - black hole

cyr: Names of fairy-tale characters in Serbian
note:
Names of fairy-tale characters in Serbian:
• Ру̑жно па̏че - The Ugly Duckling
• Пепѐљуга - Cinderella
• Снежана - Snow White
• Мала сирена - The Little Mermaid
• Палчица - Thumbelina
• Снежна краљица - The Snow Queen
• Принцеза на зрну грашка - The Princess and the Pea

In Serbia only children's cartoons are dubbed; films for adults are shown with subtitles.

cyr: Перица - the hero of Serbian jokes
note:
The boy Пѐрица is the Serbian counterpart of Little Johnny. His jokes can be childish or rude, but in children's collections they are simple and suitable for beginner reading.

A typical pun: in an English lesson Перица calls the rooms ливингрум, батрум, по̀друм, because по̀друм (basement) also ends in "-rum", like "room".

In a Serbian film in a southern dialect you can hear:
• the stress does not move forward (готово, ПАцови; the stressed syllable is written with a capital letter)
• few cases: ти си у ту секту instead of ти си у то̑ј се̑ктӣ
• other words: убаво (beautiful), збо̀рити (to speak), шта работиш

The future tense: ће comes first, without да: ће ви̏дӣш, ће се видимо.

A dialect in Serbia is normal and not stigmatized.

cyr: Anglicisms are written as they sound

related.en: to hate on someone, to troll

note:
Serbian spelling is phonetic, so English words are written as they sound:
• фјучерс (futures)
• хепиенд (happy end)
• хе̏јтовати (to hate)
• серчовати (to search)
• даунлоудовати (to download)

Adapting a foreign word to Serbian is called посрбљавање. There is a dictionary of new anglicisms with about 4,500 words.

Slang loves exaggeration and comparisons with objects:
• вугла - head; the syllables are swapped from гла́ва, which is how ша̏тровачкӣ го̏во̄р works
• њу̏шка, фа̑ца - mug, face
• радари - ears (radars)
• ка̏нџе - nails (claws)
• ви̏ле - hands (pitchforks)
• фарови - eyes (headlights)
• кљу̑н - beak (nose or mouth)
• чука - heart
• гиљарке - legs

Much of it sounds rude or jokey.

Word-for-word translation leads to mistakes:
• де̏сити се takes the dative: шта му се десило - what happened to him
• лепа идеја simply means «a good idea»
• in speech где (where) is often used instead of куда (where to): где идеш? for куда идеш?

Which case a verb takes has to be learned for each verb.

Space in Serbian:
• Ме̏се̄ц - the Moon
• све̏мӣр - the universe
• помра̀че̄ње - eclipse
• сазвѐжђе - constellation
• небеско тело - celestial body
• Сунчев систем - the Solar System
• ва̏здӯшнӣ омо̀та̄ч - atmosphere
• Вѐликӣ Мѐдвед and Ма̏лӣ Мѐдвед - the Big and Little Dipper (Ursa Major and Minor)
• Севе́рњача - Polaris, the North Star
• месечеве мене - phases of the Moon

Children go to вр̀тић, then to основна школа (8 years), then to средња школа: a gymnasium or a vocational school (стручна школа).

There is no separate primary school: people say нижи разреди основне школе (the lower grades).

The school-leaving exam is мату́ра, and a graduate is ма̀турант.

Schools are often named after writers and scholars, for example "Вук Караџић".

cyr: Craftsmen instead of a one-stop service center
note:
Serbia has no single "service center": services are provided by individual craftsmen in kiosks around the city:
• shoes are repaired by an о̀бућа̄р
• keys are copied by a кључар or бра̏ва̄р
• watches are repaired by a ча̀со̄внича̄р
• jewelry - зла̀та̄р
• clothes are altered by a кро̀ја̄ч
• fur - кр̀зна̄р
• knives are sharpened by an о̏штрач

Thread and needles are sold at a позамантерија (haberdashery).

In autumn people in Serbia put up зимница for the winter.

Spreads:
• а̀јва̄р, made of roasted peppers, is the king of spreads: бла̑гӣ (mild) or љу̑тӣ (hot)
• пѝнђур - eggplant spread
• љутѐница - hot pepper relish

Vegetables are pickled: ту̀ршија, кисели краставци, ки̏селӣ ку̀пус.

Sweets: сла̀тко̄ (fruit preserves, for example од ви̏ша̄ња̄), пѐкмез, мармела́да.

related.en: Well, now you can sit there

note:
A short «е̏» at the start of a phrase is very common in Serbian dialogue. Klajn's dictionary describes dozens of its meanings.

With it you can:
• call someone over - «Е̏, де̏во̄јко!»
• sigh - «Е, ко би рекао»
• admire - «Е, што је лепа!»
• agree - «Е̏, па до̀бро»
• sum things up - «Е, сад седи»
• start a new topic or warn someone - «Е, пази!»

cyr: Божић is not quite the same as Christmas
note:
The English word Christmas is usually translated as Бо̀жић, but the traditions behind them are different.

In Serbia, Christmas falls on January 7 and there are no presents under the tree: the јелка is decorated for New Year.

On Christmas people:
• burn oak branches - ба̏дња̄к
• go to church
• say Христос се роди!
• wait for the положајник - the first guest of the year

New Year decorations in Serbian are новогодишњи украси.

related.en: St Tryphon, patron saint of winegrowers

note:
St Valentine's Day in Serbia is Дан заљубљених. People feel differently about it:
• some consider it foreign to Orthodoxy
• others joke about it
• others are indifferent

Shops, however, are happy to run promotions.

For Orthodox believers this is the day of Све̑тӣ Три̏фӯн, the patron saint of winegrowers.

The greeting: Срећан Дан заљубљених!

In everyday speech Serbs liberally pad their sentences with connecting words that are not in textbooks:
• ми̏слӣм - «I mean»
• ка̏о - «like»
• ово оно - «this and that»

There is no direct translation: they are just pause fillers. When you hear them, do not try to translate them literally, but catch the meaning around them.

cyr: Вуков споменик is not a monument to a wolf

related.en: a district of Belgrade named after the monument to Vuk

note:
Ву̑к is not only «wolf» but also a personal name: children were given it as a protective charm.

Vuk Stefanović Karadžić (1787-1864):
• reformed the writing system on the principle «write as you speak»
• created the modern alphabet
• collected folk songs and proverbs

A street and schools are named after him. In Belgrade there is a district called Вуков споменик, named after the monument to Vuk (спо̏менӣк means «monument»).

cyr: Phrases for when something breaks at home

related.en: The switch needs to be replaced.
The boiler needs to be repaired.
I need to hang the mirror.
Water is leaking from the faucet.
The light bulb has burned out.

note:
What needs to be done:
• replace - Тре́ба заме́нити прекѝда̄ч
• repair - Тре́ба по̀правити ко̀тао
• hang - Треба да окачим огледало

How to explain what is broken:
• Цури вода из чесме
• Прегорела је сијалица
• Запушила се цев
• Не ра̏ди пе̑ћ

A request to the repairman: Молим вас да прикључите ...

cyr: Small things for the kitchen and home
note:
Names of household items that are not in textbooks:
• подметач - trivet
• цѐдиљка - colander
• сецкалица за поврће - vegetable chopper
• оцеђивач за судове - dish rack
• ка̀луп за ле̑д - ice cube tray
• мерна чаша - measuring cup
• четка за ВЦ - toilet brush
• пр̀скалица - spray bottle

Ку̏ка is simply a hook, and кр̏па is a rag and also a kitchen towel.

related.en: cream slice (custard between layers of puff pastry)
meringue cream on a sponge base
Jaffa Cakes (sponge cookies with orange jelly and chocolate)

note:
Pastry-shop classics:
• кре̏мпита - a thick layer of cream between layers of puff pastry
• шампита - fluffy white meringue cream on a sponge base
• принцес крофна - a cream puff

Turkish cuisine left behind туфа̀хија (apples in syrup with walnuts), када́иф, орашница and су̏тлија̄ш.

From store-bought sweets: јафа кејк, бананица, наполитанке.

Тулумбе are little fingers of dough soaked in syrup.

cyr: How to describe pain to a doctor
note:
Бо̑л is masculine in Serbian, so adjectives with it are masculine too.

How to describe pain:
• by strength: сла̏б, у̀мерен, ја̑к, непо̀дношљив
• by duration: про́лазан, у̏по̄ран, хро̀ничан, и̏знена̄дан
• by character: ту̑п, о̏штар, пулси́рајӯћи, уба́дајӯћи, пѐкӯћи

The pain comes in attacks: бол се јавља у нападима.

Unpleasant sensations in general - те̏гобе, cramps - гр̀чеви, pins and needles - трнци.

cyr: How Serbs communicate on social media

related.sr: Тражим стан, Нови Београд, до 400 евра, непушачи, без кућних љубимаца
related.en: Looking for an apartment, New Belgrade, up to 400 euros, non-smokers, no pets
related.acc: Тра̏жим ста̑н, Но̏ви Бео̀град, до 400 е̏вра, непу̀шачи, без ку̏ћних љу̀бӣма̄ца̄

note:
Three things give away a foreigner on Serbian social media:
• Serbs use real emoji rather than typed smileys
• they love sending стикере in reply to До̀бро ју̏тро!
• housing ads are short and to the point, without family photos or self-introductions

An example: Тражим стан, Нови Београд, до 400 евра, непушачи, без кућних љубимаца

The basics:
• сло̏во - letter, ре̑ч - word
• гла̑с - sound
• са̏могласнӣк, су̀гласнӣк - vowel, consonant
• на́гласак - accent, а̀кценат - stress

Parts of speech: и̏меница, за̑меница, при́дев, гла̏гол, при́лог, пре́длог, ве̑знӣк, ре̏чца, у̏звӣк.

Categories: ро̑д, бро̑ј (једнѝна, множѝна), па́деж.

There are seven cases, the last of them the vocative, and their names are Latin-based: но̏минатӣв, ге̏нитӣв, да́тӣв, а̏кузатӣв, и̏нструмента̄л, ло̏катӣв, во̏катӣв.

cyr: How people speak, as opposed to how they write
note:
In fast speech Serbs shorten words:
• ишао - ишо
• ви̑део - видо
• да урадим - дурадим

That is how people talk, but not how they write: in writing the full forms remain.

Sometimes Serbs jokingly write down the colloquial pronunciation, and such spelling is hard to decipher.

cyr: The first Bible translations into the vernacular
note:
In the 19th century the New Testament was translated into the vernacular by Vuk Karadžić and the Old Testament by Đura Daničić. This was an important step for the Serbian literary language.

Many biblical expressions are still alive in the language, although they contain a lot of archaic forms:
• the ending -ога: ближњега свога
• the participle вапијући
• the verb иштите

related.sr: Чак Норис може да дели и нулом
related.en: Chuck Norris can even divide by zero
related.acc: Ча̏к Но̏рис мо̏же да де̏ли и ну̏лом

related.sr: Кад Чак Норис сече лук, не плаче он, него лук
related.en: When Chuck Norris cuts an onion, it is not him who cries but the onion
related.acc: Ка̏д Ча̏к Но̏рис се̏че лу̏к, не пла̑че о̑н, не̏го лу̏к

note:
In Serbia, «Chuck Norris facts» have become part of the folklore of jokes (ви̏ц), next to the heroes Перица, Мујо and Хасо.

They are short exaggerations about an all-powerful hero:
• Чак Норис може да дели и нулом
• Кад Чак Норис сече лук, не плаче он, него лук

In colloquial Serbian, things are often named after the people they are associated with:
• титовка - a partisan cap with a star
• ленинка - a peaked cap
• фа̀нто̄мка - a balaclava
• исусовке - strappy sandals
• тарзанка - a hairstyle with short sides
• ленонке - round glasses
• терминаторке - high sneakers
• спенсерице - light lace-up boots

These names are informal.

Many cities sound different from their English names:
• Мѝнхен, Па̀рӣз, Марсеј, Мила̑но
• На́пуљ, Фиренца, Бе̑ч
• Брѝсел, Бу̏курешт, Даблин

Gender: Бу̀димпешта is feminine, while Пра̏г, Казањ and Перм are masculine: у Казању, из Казања, до Перма.

cyr: Phrases from a Serbian childhood in the 90s

related.en: Come here, I won't do anything to you

related.sr: Остави те колаче, то је за госте
related.en: Leave those cakes alone, they are for the guests
related.acc: Оста̀ви те ко̀лаче, то̑ је за го̏сте

related.en: Can Milica come out to play?

related.sr: Нарезаћу ти на ЦД омиљене песме
related.en: I'll burn your favorite songs onto a CD for you
related.acc: Нарѐзаћу ти на ЦД омѝљене пе̏сме

related.en: Call me, I don't have enough credit

note:
Serbs now in their forties remember the 90s through phrases:
• Дођи, нећу ти ништа - the parental «threat»
• Остави те колаче, то је за госте - the best is kept for guests
• Може ли Милица напоље? - asking parents to let a child out to play
• Нарезаћу ти на ЦД омиљене песме
• Назови ме, немам довољно кредита

These are recognizable marks of the time: childhood on the street, discs, cassettes and prepaid phones.

The colloquial ћа̑о (both «hi» and «bye») traveled this way:
1. Medieval Latin sclavus - «Slav», later «slave».
2. Venetian s-ciavo - «I am your servant».
3. Italian ciao.
4. Serbian ћа̑о.

The formula «I am your servant» gradually turned into a greeting. The native Slavic counterpart is здра̏во.

cyr: Јао and јој: not only negative
note:
The interjections ја̏о and јој are not limited to «oh no». Depending on intonation and context they express:
• annoyance - Јао, заборавила сам телефон!
• delight - Ја̏о, што̏ је ле̑по!, Јој, преслатко!

Only ја̏о takes the dative: Ја̏о мѐнӣ!, Јао онима који...

related.en: exam at the end of elementary school

note:
The school system in Serbia:
1. вр̀тић - kindergarten.
2. The zero grade and основна школа (grades 1-8).
3. Гѝмна̄зија or стручна школа.

The school year is divided into two полугодишта, with a зи̑мскӣ ра́спуст and a летњи распуст.

At the end of elementary and secondary school students take the малу матуру and the матуру.

The class monitor is the председник одељења.

cyr: What foreigners find hard to pronounce
note:
What foreigners find hard to pronounce:
• long words: државља́нство, посластѝчарница
• the syllabic «Р» among other consonants: твр̀ђава, стр̏шље̄н, нерђајући челик, чвр̏шћӣ
• the soft «Љ», a single sound like «lli» in «million»: љу̀ља̄шка
• unstressed «О», which stays a clear «О» and is not reduced: по̀сао, по̀родица

The 3rd person plural pronoun has three forms, by gender:
• о̀ни - masculine
• оне - feminine
• она - neuter

The endings match the plural of nouns of the same gender:
• при̏јатељи - они - добри
• девојке - оне - лепе
• дѐца - она - вредна

Де́те is neuter, so дѐца is «она». A mixed group of men and women is «они».

Family is important in Balkan culture, so there are many words for relatives.
• father's brother - стри̑ц
• mother's brother - у̏ја̄к
• an aunt, on either side - те̏тка

The uncles' wives have their own names too: стри̑на, у̏јна.

A grandmother may affectionately call a girl си̑не as well.

Almost every profession has a separate word for a man and for a woman: лѐка̄р - лѐкарка.

These double forms developed in the language and a few years ago were made official in the norm. So lists of professions have twice as many words.

A nationality has separate words for a man, a woman, the plural and the language: Ср̏бин, Ср̏пкиња, Срби, ср̏пскӣ.

The name of the language is written with a small letter, the other forms with a capital (unlike in English).

To answer the question «where?» you need the locative: Жи́вӣм у Нѐмачко̄ј.

cyr: Syllable games and dropping «х» in colloquial speech
note:
In colloquial Serbian, syllables are sometimes swapped as a joke: тра̀фика becomes фикатра.

In dialects the «х» is also often lost:
• ладно instead of хла́дно
• леб instead of хле̏б
• оћеш instead of хоћеш

So be ready for such forms.

related.en: How fast does a little peach run?

note:
In winter in Serbia people take out пичигузе - small plastic sleds with a handle, which children and adults ride down hills.

By a joking etymology, the word is made of пичити (to rush, to dash) and гуз (backside): «a rushing backside».

There is also a pun: Колико брзо трчи мала бресква? - Peachy. The English «peachy» sounds like «пичи».

cyr: Плава коса is not blue hair
note:
Пла̑в means both «blue» and «blond»: пла̑ва ко̀са is light hair, blond, and the sky and the sea are also «плаво».

In Old Slavic «плав» described what is light, pale or golden. For blue there used to be the words мо̏дар and си̑њӣ: модро море.

The meaning depends on the context.

The standard Serbian accent combines pitch and stress: a syllable stands out not only by force but also by tone.

It can be long or short, rising or falling - four types in all: ру́ка, жѐна, ма̑јка, бра̏т.

Tone and length can tell words apart: гра̑д «city» and гра̑д «hail».

In everyday speech many people speak more simply, with a single stress accent, and are understood. Variants like ауто́бус are acceptable.

Serbia was part of the Ottoman Empire for several centuries, and thousands of Turkish words entered the language. Half of them are obsolete, but about three thousand are alive in daily life:
• ја̀стук, ко̀мшија, ба́шта
• ра̀кија, сѝрће, ка̀фа
• шѐћер, бу̀рек

Often a «Slavic» variant exists alongside, but the Turkism sounds more natural.

cyr: Countries, peoples and languages: the capital letter
note:
In Serbian, the names of countries and their inhabitants are written with a capital letter, but the language is not (unlike in English).

For each country there is a masculine and a feminine form for the inhabitant, and an adjective:
• Ср̀бија - Ср̏бин - Ср̏пкиња - ср̏пскӣ
• Нѐмачка̄ - Не́мац - Нѐмица - нѐмачкӣ
• Ки́на - Кѝне̄з - Кѝне̄скиња - кѝне̄скӣ
• Ѐнгле̄ска̄ - Ѐнгле̄з - Ѐнглескиња - ѐнгле̄скӣ

cyr: How to address people: ти or ви
note:
Serbs switch from ви̑ to ти quickly: even a shop cashier may say ћа̑о.

Formally, one says господине / госпођо / госпођице + surname in the vocative: господине Јовановићу. It is also fine without a surname.

Мо̀мак and дѐво̄јка are not used as forms of address.

related.en: a film without a happy ending

note:
Figurative expressions about Russia in colloquial speech:
• руска салата - Russian salad (Olivier)
• руска зима - very severe cold
• ру̏скӣ фи̏лм - a film without a happy ending, where the hero loses everything

These are stereotypes: it is useful to know them, but do not take them for neutral words.

related.en: a metal baking lid, covered with embers
a dish baked under a сач

note:
Јело испод сача is a dish that is slowly cooked under a сач: a metal lid covered with hot coals.

Most often it is meat with vegetables, for example тѐлетина or ја̀гњетина. The dish is considered home cooking and festive food.

related.en: first floor (second floor by American count)

note:
An address usually includes:
• the street and the house number
• у̀лаз (entrance)
• спра̏т (floor)
• ста̑н (apartment)
• по̏штанскӣ бро̑ј (postal code) and the city

The ground floor is при́зе̄мље: it does not count as a спра̏т (it is the zero one). So пр̀вӣ спра̏т is already the second floor by American count.

The intercom is и̏нтерфон, its code is ши̏фра.

On a walk with a dog you hear:
• дођи - come
• седи - sit
• ста̏ни - stop
• чекај - wait
• пу̑стӣ - drop it
• ти̏хо - quiet
• ха̀јде - let's go

For praise people say је л тако or бра̏во.

These are everyday words, and they work in ordinary speech too.

related.en: bogeywoman, a forest witch with a horn

note:
Бабаро́га is a character of Serbian ба̑јкӣ, related to the Russian Baba Yaga: an old forest вѐштица with a horn on her forehead, who lives in dark caves.

She is used to scare children, and by one version she comes to sleeping children at night.

The word ба̏ба here means «old woman».

In messages Serbs write in the Latin alphabet and abbreviate words:
• vrv - ве̏рова̄тно
• msm - ми̏слӣм
• nmg - не мо̀гу
• nzm - не зна̑м

The abbreviations are clear if you know the full form. Cyrillic is rarely seen in such messages.

cyr: Kinds of milk in the store
note:
Names for shopping:
• чоколадно млеко - chocolate
• млеко у праху - powdered
• кондензовано млеко - condensed
• биљно млеко - plant-based
• млеко без лактозе - lactose-free

Plant-based kinds are named after their base: сојино, бадемово, пиринчано, кокосово.

Baby formula is фо̑рмула за бебе́.

Fingers of the hand:
• па̏лац - thumb
• ка̀жипрст - index finger
• сре̏дњӣ пр̏ст - middle finger
• домали прст - ring finger
• ма̏лӣ пр̏ст - little finger

Пр̏ст means both a finger and a toe: ножни прст.

The nail is но̏кат.

cyr: An umbrella against rain and against sun
note:
Ки̏шобра̄н consists of ки̏ша (rain) and бра́нити (to defend): «protection from rain».

The same pattern gives су̏нцобра̄н - a sunshade, a beach umbrella.

Note the connecting «о».

Titles of books and films often sound different in Serbian:
• «Gone with the Wind» - Прохујало с вихором
• «Crime and Punishment» - Зло̀чин и ка̏зна
• «The Lord of the Rings» - Госпо̀да̄р прстено́ва̄
• «Poverty Is No Vice» - Сирома́штво нѝје по̀рок

A good way to remember new words.

cyr: Native language and names of languages
note:
Ма̀те̄рњӣ јѐзик - native language.

Names of languages are written with a small letter (unlike in English) and end in -ски:
• ру̏скӣ, у̀крајӣнскӣ, белоруски, јѐрме̄нскӣ
• ѐнгле̄скӣ, нѐмачкӣ, фра̀нцӯскӣ, италѝја̄нскӣ
• грузијски, албански, фи̑нскӣ, пољски
• ту̀рскӣ, гр̏чкӣ, сло̀веначкӣ, макѐдо̄нскӣ

Fairy tales in Serbian often have different titles from English:
• «Sleeping Beauty» - Успавана лепотица
• «Little Red Riding Hood» - Црвенкапа
• «Tom Thumb» - Тома Палчић
• «Cinderella» - Пепѐљуга

This helps to remember the words лепо̀тица and успавана.

related.en: meat roasted on a spit (suckling pig, lamb)
a restaurant serving roast meat; a spit oven

note:
Пѐче̄ње is meat roasted on a spit, usually a suckling pig or a lamb.

A cookie or biscuit is ке̏кс.

A place that roasts meat is called a печѐњара, and so is the spit oven itself.

Loved ones are affectionately called: ср̏це, ду́ша, ме̑д, зве́зда, зла̑то, су̑нце, ма́ца, бе́ба, мала.

Such words are used both in direct address and in conversation.

Beer can be та̑мно (dark), све̏тло (light) or точено (draft).

Wine: бело (white), црно (red), ро̀зе ви́но, домаће (homemade).

Spirits: ра̀кија, во̑тка, ви̏ски, ко̏ња̄к, вѐрмут.

On November 11 Serbia marks Armistice Day of the First World War. It is a не̏радни да̑н.

The symbol of the day is the flower Наталијина рамонда, which «resurrects» after a drought.

Vocabulary for the day: се̏ћа̄ње, јунаци.

Serbs fill pauses with words:
• зна̏чи - «so»
• па - «well»
• о̀ва̄ј - «uh», «what's-it-called»
• ми̏слӣм - «I mean»
• бу̏ква̄лно - often just for emphasis

They occur in almost every conversation.

In Serbia blood types are marked with the international system: O, A, B, AB and the Rh factor - позитивна or негативна.

For example: «O позитивна» is O positive, «AB негативна» is AB negative.

related.en: roast suckling pig on a spit

note:
On a New Year's table in Serbia you usually find:
• пѐче̄ње - roast suckling pig
• руска салата
• а̀јва̄р
• пита са сиром
• ку̏лен, ка̀јмак
• бакла̀ва
• ва̀нилице
• сла̀тко̄ од шљи̏ва
• са̀рма

related.en: oak branch that is burned in the evening

note:
Бадњи дан (January 6) is Christmas Eve. People bring a ба̏дња̄к into the house - an oak branch that is burned in the evening.

The table is meatless: па̀сӯљ, ри̏ба, ораси.

For Бо̀жић people bake a чесница with a coin in it.

On the three Sundays before Christmas family members are «tied up»:
• Детињци - children
• Материце - mothers
• О̀ци - fathers

The ransom is sweets and presents.

Некрштени дани is the period from Christmas to Богојављење (January 19).

By tradition, Christ is not yet baptized, the border between the worlds is thin, and evil spirits roam. In the past people did not leave the house at night, protected children and pregnant women, and postponed important matters.

They protected themselves from evil forces with garlic (бе̑лӣ лу̏к), the fire of the hearth and prayer. Today this is more a part of folklore.

Serbian has separate verbs for animal sounds:
• пе́тао кукуриче
• ко̀ко̄шка кокодаче
• вра̏на грача
• пи̏ле пишти
• вра́бац цвркуће
• па̏с ла̏је̄
• кра̏ва му̑че
• о́вца блеји
• пчѐла зуји

It is best to learn the animal names and verbs in pairs.

related.en: the first coffee, served to a guest
the last coffee, a hint that it's time to go home

note:
Coffee in Serbian is ка̀фа, and it has many playful names for its taste or the occasion:
• чемѐрика - bitter, from че̏ме̄р
• дочекуша - the first one, for a guest, from до̀чекати
• сѝктеруша - the last one, a hint that it's time to go home, from сиктер
• кајмакара - very thick
• шећеруша - sweet
• шлогируша - knockout-strong, from шло̑г

Ћева̀пи and плѐскавица are tourist food, not everyday meals.

At home Serbs more often cook:
• бора̀нија, гра́шак with meat
• па̏прика̄ш, ђу̀веч, са̀тараш
• пуњена паприка, са̀рма, муса̀ка

The fridge usually holds сла̀нина, коба̀сица, па̀влака, си̏р, пѐкмез and паште́та.

The obligatory first course at lunch is су̏па.

Serbian uses one word, навлака, for both a pillowcase and a duvet cover:
• навлака за јастук - a pillowcase, also called ја̀стучница
• навлака за јорган - a duvet cover

Јо̀рган is the duvet itself.

cyr: How rooms and floors are counted in rental listings

related.en: two-room apartment: a living room and a bedroom
three-room apartment: a living room and two bedrooms
the 1st floor above the ground (US: second floor)
the 2nd floor above the ground (US: third floor)

note:
Listings count rooms by the living space, not the bedrooms:
• једно̀собан - a one-room apartment, like a studio
• дво̀собан - a living room and a bedroom
• тро̀собан - a living room and two bedrooms

Floors are counted from the ground floor:
• при́зе̄мље - the ground floor
• пр̀вӣ спра̏т - the 1st floor above it (US: second floor)
• дру̏гӣ спра̏т - the 2nd floor above it (US: third floor)

Utilities are ре̏жије, rent is кѝрија or стана̀рина.

cyr: Туцање јајима: egg tapping at Easter

related.en: to tap eggs against each other

note:
At У̏скрс Serbs tap dyed eggs against each other: two people knock the tips together, and whoever's egg cracks loses.

When visiting, it is customary to bring an egg for the hosts, and the loser gives his egg to the winner.

There are even tournaments, called Туцанијада.

The verb: туцати јајима, туцамо - "we tap eggs".

Serbia has no kulich or paskha.

In the morning people eat dyed eggs, ку̏вана шу̑нка, по̀гача, си̏р, ка̀јмак, ку̏лен, мла̑д лу̏к and ро̀тквица. Bread is not taken to church, only the eggs are blessed.

The main dish of the lunch is јагњеће печење, with крофне, орехњача or мако̀вњача and пи̏та са ја̏букама for dessert.

cyr: Where the words for sushi and seafood come from
note:
Пѝринач and сѝрће came from Turkish.

Ко̀зице is the ordinary word for shrimp, literally "little goats". Гамбори is more often heard in Croatia and Slovenia, and шка̏мпи are langoustines with claws.

The other words: јѐгуља, да̏гња, штапићи.

The adjective ки̏сео is broader than "sour":
• ки̏селӣ ку̀пус - sauerkraut
• ки̏селӣ кра̏ставац - pickled cucumber
• кисела вода - sparkling mineral water
• кисела киша - acid rain
• ки̏селӣ о̏сме̄х - a forced, insincere smile

Some words have a masculine and a feminine variant, both equally correct:
• мѝнӯт and мину́та
• сѐкунд and секу̀нда
• ли̏тар and ли̏тра
• палачи́нак and палачи́нка
• ко̀верат and ко̀ве̄рта

Sometimes the difference is one of style or region, but more often there is none, and both variants are heard equally.

cyr: What people drink in Serbia in summer
note:
The classics for hot weather:
• шпри̏цер - white wine with sparkling or plain water
• сок од зове - a drink made from elderflower syrup
• сок од вишње
• лимуна́да - water with lemon and sugar or honey
• ле̏денӣ ча̏ј, точено пиво

Кисела вода is sparkling water, often with lemon.

In messages people use abbreviations:
• vrv - ве̏рова̄тно
• msm - ми̏слӣм
• nmg - не мо̀гу
• nzm - не зна̑м
• nmj - не̏мој

This is colloquial chat style; it is not used in formal letters.

cyr: The suffix -оница: a place of action
note:
From verbs and nouns Serbian forms names of places with the suffix -оница: учио́ница, радио́ница, перѝоница, залагао́ница.

Once you know this suffix, the meaning of a new word can often be guessed.

Serbian has separate words for different kinds of packaging:
• конзѐрва - a tin can: fish, pâté
• лѝме̄нка - a metal can: soda, beer
• те́гла - a glass jar: jam, honey, ajvar
• фла̏ша, ку̀тија, ке̏са, ке̏сица, џа̑к
• ка̀рто̄н - a large box

Serbs speak about weight gently:
• бу̏цмаст, буцмаста - affectionate, mostly about babies and chubby cheeks
• пунији, пунија - neutral, about adults who are on the fuller side
• елегантно попуњен (-а) - jokingly refined, implies dignity and style

Ottoman rule left words for daily life, trade and crafts: са̑т, ча̏к, ба̀рем, ћо̀шак, ку́ла, џа́мија, ђу̏бре, ме̏рмер, ѐксер, чѐлик, ба̀кар, за̀на̄т, ма̀рама, џе̏п.

They stuck because they were handy, had no equivalent, and became part of the culture.

Words about food and household items are in the first collection.

related.en: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

note:
Serbian titles are often translated, not copied:
• Пепѐљуга - "Cinderella"
• Снежана и седам патуљака - "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs"
• Лепо̀тица и зве̑р - "Beauty and the Beast"
• Мала сирена - "The Little Mermaid"
• Кра̑љ ла̏во̄ва̄ - "The Lion King"
• Маза и луња - "Lady and the Tramp"

The last one's title conveys the characters: ма̏за is a pampered favorite, луња is a street tramp.

In autumn Serbia switches to зимско време: the clocks go back an hour, and the time difference with other countries changes.

Useful expressions:
• поме́рати са̑т
• временска разлика
• временска зона

The word вре́ме means both time and weather.

cyr: Slava: the family patron saint's day

related.en: slava, the family's patron saint's day
to a slava, as a guest

note:
Сла̏ва is the Serbian celebration of a family's patron saint (све́тац). On December 19 many people celebrate Ни̏кољдан, St Nicholas' Day.

The family prays and lays a table with bread and fish, because it falls in a fasting period. The slava is celebrated at home, so shopping malls are empty that day.

The greeting is Срећна слава!

A joke: half of Serbia celebrates its slava, the other half goes to a slava as guests.

related.en: the Moscow cake (from a Belgrade hotel)
a sponge cake soaked in three kinds of milk

note:
What to try:
• торта «Мо̏сква» from a Belgrade hotel
• трилече - a sponge cake soaked in three kinds of milk
• бајадѐра, кре̏мпита, урмашице
• сла̀тко̄, ва̀нилице, бакла̀ва, слатка пита

The Moscow cake was invented in Belgrade, not in Russia.

related.en: the first coffee, for a guest

note:
Coffee in Serbian is ка̀фа. Colloquial speech has invented many nicknames for it, and each one describes the taste or the situation right away:
• чемѐрика - bitter, from че̏ме̄р
• дочекуша - the first one, for a guest, from до̀чекати
• сѝктеруша - the last one, a hint that it's time to go home, from сиктер
• кајмакара - very thick
• шећеруша or шербетуша - sweet
• шлогируша - so strong it nearly gives you a stroke, from шло̑г

cyr: What Serbs really eat at home
note:
Serbia is seen as a land of meat eaters, but at home people eat many vegetable and side dishes that are not on tourist menus.

The fridge usually holds сла̀нина, коба̀сица, па̀влака, си̏р, пѐкмез and паште́та.

Favorite home dishes:
• бора̀нија, гра́шак, пѝла̄в
• са̀тараш, па̏прика̄ш, муса̀ка
• пуњена паприка
• са̀рма - New Year is not complete without it

The first course at lunch is almost always су̏па.

related.en: Serbian coffee brewed in a cezve

note:
The national strong drink is ра̀кија: plum, grape or apricot.

Медо̀вача is a sweet rakija with honey, softer and more aromatic. Шумадијски чај is actually hot rakija with sugar, served in winter.

Among soft drinks, the sparkling mineral water «Кне̑з Мѝлош» is popular.

The most recognizable symbol is домаћа кафа, brewed in a cezve, with a thick foam on top.

related.en: the red egg, the guardian of the house

note:
On Вѐликӣ пе́так Serbs dye Easter eggs (фарбати јаја), and the first one is always red. It is called чува̀ркућа - "the guardian of the house".

The egg is kept until the next Easter: it is believed to protect the family from misfortune.

When the new Easter comes, the old egg is buried in the ground or given to a river. If there is no river nearby, it is flushed down the toilet with running water.

Serbia has no kulich or paskha: the word У̏скрс means only the holiday itself.

In the morning people eat dyed eggs, кувана шунка, по̀гача, си̏р, ка̀јмак, пр̀шут, ку̏лен, мла̑д лу̏к and ро̀тквица. Bread is not taken to church: after the liturgy only the eggs are blessed.

Lunch is roast ја̏гње and appetizers (пре̏дјело), with крофне, пи̏та са ја̏букама and мако̀вњача for dessert.

The family gathers at one table, all generations together.

related.en: cheekbone; fingertip pad; a little strawberry

note:
Ја̏года in Serbian means only a strawberry. Berries in general are called бобичасто воће, literally "berry fruit".

Summer at the market:
• ја̏года, ма̀лина, боро́вница
• ку̀пина, ри̏бӣзла
• тре̏шња, ви̏шња, гро̑жђе

Јаго̀дица is the cheekbone, the pad of a finger, and also a "little strawberry".

cyr: Money in Serbian: from novac to kinta
note:
The basic word for "money" is но̀вац, and па̏ре comes second. Both fit everywhere except official documents.

Cash: ке̏ш, готовѝна. Tip: ба̀кшиш.

Slang: ло́ва, ки̑нта, ди̏нџа. Ки̑нта comes from the Albanian qindarkë, a small coin.

Examples: пу̏н је па̏ра, дугујеш ми кинту, нисам при кинти.

Many animals have their own word for the young, and it is neuter: штѐне, ма̏че, тѐле, ждре̑бе, ја̏гње, ја̏ре, пра̑се, пи̏ле, па̏че, ла̏не, ме̏че.

Don't mix up ја̏ре with ја̏рац - that is an adult billy goat.

The universal word is младу́нче: младунче лава - a lion cub.

Serbian cakes have telling names:
• Срнећа леђа - a walnut sponge with chocolate glaze
• Мо̏сква шни̏т - the signature of the hotel «Москва»: vanilla cream, cherry, pineapple and almonds
• Васина торта - walnuts, orange and chocolate; by legend the recipe was invented by the mother-in-law of a man named Vasa from Параћин
• Реформ торта - chocolate and walnut; the name is linked to the socialist reforms in Yugoslavia

Слага̀лица is a beloved Serbian TV quiz show, based on the French show "Des chiffres et des lettres". It has eight rounds.

The host Milka Canić always opened simply: До̀бро ве̏че̄! - everyone knows this phrase.

There is also a morning counterpart: Бео̀граде, до̀бро ју̏тро. It was the name of a program by the writer and journalist Duško Radović, which aired on «Студио Б» in 1975-1982.

cyr: What the shapes in coffee grounds mean
note:
In гледање у шољу people look at the shapes the та́лог left at the bottom of the cup.

Birds:
• го̏лӯб - good luck
• ла̏бӯд - success
• ла́ста - don't rush decisions
• о̀рао - a change for the better
• га̏вра̄н - bad news
• гу̏ска - you will find a solution

Animals:
• ма̏чка - a quarrel and deceit
• па̏с - a faithful friend
• о́вца - happiness
• пра̑се - temptation and prosperity
• ко̏њ - good income
• зе̑ц - speed or shame

Elements: во̀да - money, ва̏тра - be careful.

cyr: Native words and Turkisms: who was displaced

related.en: a word with the root чест
old word for a water source
"black one" (monks were called so for their clothes)

note:
Many ordinary words came from Turkish and displaced Slavic ones:
• ка̀пија - replaced вратнице (wicker gates)
• са̀пӯн - replaced ми̏ло (from ми̏ти, "to wash", compare уми́вати)
• ча́мац - replaced чу̑н
• пѐшкӣр - replaced ру̀чнӣк and о̏тарак
• па́рче and ко̀ма̄д - replaced the old че̑ст, which survives in чѐшња̄к and причестити се
• ђу̏бре - took the place of гно̑ј
• бу̀на̄р - replaced студе́нац and кла̏денац
• че̏сма - took the place of то̏чка

Мо̀нах and ка̀луђер both come from Greek: they named the people who used to be called цр̀нац because of their black clothes.

cyr: Serbian folklore creatures: Baš Čelik and others

related.en: Baš Čelik, a Serbian folk villain

note:
Ба̏ш-Чѐлик ("steel head" in Turkish) is a character of folk tales: a very strong, almost invulnerable giant who kidnaps beautiful girls.

Некрштенци are souls of children who died unbaptized: at night they fly as birds and drink the milk of cows and sheep.

A вукодлак can be an unborn child of a pregnant woman who died, if an animal runs over the grave.

Псоглавци are creatures with a human body and a dog's head.

Ба̏бица used to mean "midwife"; now it means an obstetric nurse.

Betting shops are on every corner in Serbia, so the betting vocabulary comes in handy.

Cards: карте in a шпил are де̑ле (dealt) and мешају (shuffled). Коцкице бацају - dice are thrown.

Bets:
• у́лог - a stake in a game
• о̏пклада - a wager
• кво́та - the bookmaker's odds

Results: доби́так - winnings, губи́так - a loss.

Cards by value: десетка, дѐве̄тка, осмица, сѐдмица, шестица. Блефи́рати - to bluff.

cyr: Verbs of the body and not-so-elegant habits

related.en: to smack one's lips, to chew noisily

note:
Verbs of the body and not-so-elegant habits.

Sounds and physiology: хр́кати, шту̏цати, подриги́вати, ка̀шљати, ки́јати, зно̀јити се.

Nose: ду́вати но̑с, шмр̀цати, ча̏чкати но̑с.

Mouth: пљу̏вати, мља̏цкати, ба̏лавити.

Other: гри̏сти но̏кте, цедити бубуљице, пр́љати.

The Balkans have exchanged words for centuries, and part of the everyday vocabulary came from Greek. Many words sound almost the same as their Greek counterparts: ти̏гањ, тр̀пеза, ха̀ртија, крѐвет, лѝвада.

Through the church came ѝкона and ма̏настӣр.

From the kitchen and home: бѝбер, сто̏ма̄к - not the organ, but the belly.

cyr: The root red: order, row, queue
note:
The word ре̑д covers order, queue, row and layer at once. This gives a whole family:
• по̏ред
• ре̏досле̄д
• др̏воре̄д
• уре́дити
• преуредити - including rearranging furniture

So "Lady in red" sounds to a Serb like "a lady in order" (дама у реду): red in Serbian is цр̀вен.

related.en: to entertain, to get a crowd going

note:
Serbian verbs in -ирати and -овати look international, and most are easy to guess from English; note аними́рати, which is mostly about entertaining a crowd:
• ирити́рати - to irritate
• прецизирати - to specify, to clarify
• неги́рати - to deny
• аними́рати - to entertain and get a crowd going
• едуковати - to train, to educate
• ко̀мпликовати - to complicate
• инсисти́рати - to insist

Verbs in -ирати conjugate like -ам verbs: прецизирам. Verbs in -овати give -ујем: едукујем, компликујем. Most are biaspectual.

related.en: the wedding best man, the witness
the old kum, a kum across generations

note:
Ку́мство is a close bond between families, often almost like kinship.

Ку̑м can be the witness at a wedding (венчани кум) or a godfather (крштени кум). Стари кум is the one whose family has been friends with yours for generations.

The sons of kums often become kums to each other too. A kum is a friend who was chosen into the family.

related.en: how are you doing, where have you been

note:
A neutral phrase often has a more relaxed counterpart:
• не брини - ла̏гано, бре̏
• морам да идем - одох
• обична ствар - ништа спец
• ка̏ко си - где̏ си

This sounds friendly. Don't answer strangers and older people this way.

related.en: the Latin name of Novi Sad

note:
The city is abbreviated НС.

The historic nickname is Српска Атина. The Latin name is Неопланта, the Hungarian one is Újvidék.

On declension see the grammar: both parts of Нови Сад decline in Serbian.

Врбица, or Лазарева субота, is a children's holiday on the eve of Palm Sunday (Цвети).

Mothers dress the children up, put венчићи on their heads and hang звончићи on a tricolor ribbon around their necks.

In church young willow branches are blessed and then kept at home by the icon.

A playful "dictionary of sounds":
• «а» - I didn't catch that
• «е̏» - oh, come on, you're kidding
• «и» - what's so strange about it
• «о» - well, that's news
• уф - scary
• у̏х - awkward, unpleasant
• ех - it used to be like that, now it's only talked about
• ах - a missed chance
• их - if only I had known
• па - so what?
• ма̏ - never mind, forget it

The Russian TV series "The Boy's Word" was shown in Serbia under the title Часна уличарска - literally "honest street".

The title plays on the expression часна реч - "word of honor". It is a translation by meaning, not a literal one.

related.sr: Добар дан, Марија је на телефону.
related.en: Good afternoon, this is Marija (literally "Marija is on the phone").
related.acc: До̏бар да̑н, Ма̀рија је на телѐфону.

note:
People pick up the phone with Ха̏ло! or Мо̏лим!, or politely with Изволите?.

The caller introduces themselves in the third person: Добар дан, Марија је на телефону.

To ask for someone: Могу ли да добијем Стефана?

The reason for the call is stated right away: Зовем у вези са огласом.

Calls end with Ва̏жи, Договорено, Чу̏је̄мо се, А̀јде, здра̏во.

If you can't get through: Зовем, нико се не јавља.

Слага̀лица is the best-known quiz on Serbian public TV.

In one of the rounds (спојнице) you have to connect pairs: dog breeds and cartoon characters, republics and their capitals.

The philologist Милка Цанић (1944-2016), the quiz's editor and proofreader, stayed in viewers' memory with her greeting До̀бро ве̏че̄!. Say her name to a Serb and he will most likely answer with exactly that.

cyr: Where to drive, where to go: direction words
note:
Basic directions: пра́во, де̏сно, ле̑во, на̏пре̄д, на̏за̄д, го̏ре, до̏ле.

Behind the wheel: рикверц - reverse gear, у рикверц - in reverse.

About movement: цикцак, укруг.

Turned over: на̏опачке̄, наглава̀чке̄.

Watch out: пра́во means "straight ahead", not "right". "Right" is де̏сно.

The names of the planets are close to the English ones: Мѐркӯр, Вѐнера, Зѐмља, Ма̏рс, Ју̀питер, Са̀турн, У̀ра̄н, Нѐптӯн, Плу̀то̄н. Only Earth is different: Зѐмља.

The Sun is Су̑нце, the Moon is Ме̏се̄ц, and "star" is зве́зда.

Astronomy words: celestial bodies, phenomena and equipment.

Celestial bodies: коме́та, астеро̀ӣд, метѐо̄р, звезда падалица, суперно̑ва, црна рупа.

Phenomena and equipment: о̏рбита, те̏лескоп, све̏мӣрскӣ бро̑д, међузвездана прашина.

"Space" is usually све̏мӣр, and the whole Universe is Унивѐрзум.

An eclipse is помра̀че̄ње: помрачење Сунца, and a lunar eclipse is помрачење Месеца.

cyr: The Red Cross and aid: vocabulary
note:
Words found in news and appeals for help: Црвени крст, волонтер, ѝзбеглица, жр̏тва, хуманитарна помоћ, спасилачка операција, евакуа́ција, рехабилита́ција, психолошка подршка, прихватни центар.

Two phrases that both can be rendered as "emergency help":
• хитна помоћ - the ambulance service and its call-out
• прва помоћ - first aid given on the spot before doctors arrive

Breed names are mostly borrowed but spelled by Serbian rules: чивава, мопс, булдог, лабрадор, златни ретривер.

Јазавѝчар (dachshund) comes from ја̏завац ("badger"). A German shepherd is нѐмачкӣ о̀вча̄р, a poodle is пу̏дла or пу̀длица.

cyr: New Year in Serbia: the table and two holidays

related.en: the Serbian New Year, January 13 (Orthodox calendar)

note:
Serbia sees in the New Year from December 31 to January 1, and on January 13 it also celebrates the Orthodox one - Српска Нова година.

People usually celebrate at home. The table has руска салата, са̀рма, various meats, колачи and ра̀кија.

Young people gather at friends' places or go to a concert. At midnight they congratulate each other and watch the ва̏троме̄т.

On holidays people like to watch old TV series such as Сре̏ћнӣ љу̑ди.

In one legend people carried darkness out of their house in buckets because it was dark inside. Saint Sava taught them to cut windows (про́зор), and they were very grateful.

In another, a disciple's honey (ме̑д) went missing. Sava said loudly that a bee (пчѐла) would land on the thief's (ло́пов) hat that day. The thief feared it all day and gave himself away.

cyr: Signs and notices in the street
note:
Signs often use short imperative forms:
• Вуци and Гурај - "pull" and "push" on doors
• Не гази траву
• Не дирај

The rest are nouns or participles:
• Забра̏њен у̀лаз, Забрањено паркирање
• Тишѝна
• Пажња, клизаво!, Па̀жња, стѐпенице!
• Чувај се пса
• Вѝсок на́пон

cyr: A Belgrade market: Каленић and others

related.en: it was heard at the market

note:
For Serbs a пѝјаца is not just a market but a place with character: on Каленићева and Бајлонијева пијаца and at Зелени венац a person feels at home.

Каленићева пијаца opened in 1926 on land bequeathed to the city by the patron Влајко Каленић. The writer Момо Капор called it an exhibition of living still lifes.

Market words: тѐзга, гајбица, кило и по.

The expression чуло се на пијаци meant: it was heard at the market, i.e. the information is reliable even though the newspapers are silent.

Four Serbian painters:
• Паја Јовановић - the main realist, author of Кићење невесте: bridesmaids in folk costumes dress the bride for the wedding
• Надежда Петровић brought impressionism and expressionism to early 20th-century Serbia (Ко̏сово по̏ље)
• Сава Шумановић studied in Paris and combined cubism with the landscapes of Srem (Шидијанке)
• Милена Павловић-Барили, close to surrealism, worked in New York: her drawing made the cover of Vogue in April 1940

Words for talking about painting: сли̏ка̄р, пла́тно, пѐјза̄ж, потез четкицом, јарке боје.

cyr: Couriers and parcels: words and phrases

related.en: I'm in front of the building.
The intercom doesn't work, I'll let you in.
Can you leave it with a neighbor?

note:
